1/
held on July 6, 1948 between an officer of this Mission and Mr. KATAYAMA
Tetsu, President of the Social Democratic Party and former Prime
2/
Minister, and on July 7, 1948 between the same officer and Mr. MATSU:OTO
Takizo, Chairnan of the Policy Committee of the People's Cooperative
Party nd former Parliamentary Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs in
the Katayama Cabinet, on the general subject of the current political
situation and the possible course of political events this coming fall.
These and other conversations with Japanese baders have further
confirmed the instability of the Ashida Cabinet which we have previously
reported, (see this Mission's despatch No. 263 of May 5, 1948). Both
Mr. Katayama and Mr. Matsumoto expect that during the coming fall the
present cabinet will either be forced to resign and a new one be formed
or the National Diet will heve to be dissolved. These men and also
Dr. ASHIDA Hitoshi, the Prime Minister and President of the Democretic
Party, (accorcing to Mr. Metsumoto who is closely asscciated with
Dr. Ashida despite effiliation with a different party), are inclined
at this time to prefer the latter course. The main reason for this
preference anpears to be th.t these men do not wish to see the Democratic
Liberal Party form a new cabinet until this new party obtains the mandate
of the people through a general election.
It is generally relt that an extraordinery session will be called
this fall to consider a supplementary budget in view of the united
front being presented by government labor unions for a wage inerease
and other demands. Between now and that time we believe there will

There a opeared no doubt in !r. Katayama's mind that the present

devise a supplementery buaget. at that time the two "realistic"

increased above the Y379l level upon which the present budget is based.
Mr. Katayame believes that the Democratic Party will agree only upon
 reletively small increase which these two ministers cannot accept
and that they will therefore resign. Another possible cause of their
resignation mey be an attempt at revision of labor legislation.
According to Yr. Katayame, both tho left wing faction and the

ena of the last session).
The feeling is growing, Mr. Katayame thinks, thet during the
September session either the present cabinet will be forced to resign
or the Diet will be dissolved. Mr. Katayame maintained that he has
felt up until now th't the hiatus ceused by dissolution of the Diet
would be too great in Japen's present circumstances, but thet he has

One important reacon anpeared to be the possibility that the next cabinet

Mr. Katayama stated that in his opinion the majority of Diet
members are now in favor of a dissolution of the Diet to be followed
by a general election. He said that he himself with this in mind
had already covered about two-thirds of Japan trying to consolidate
the Social Democratic Party and also to inform the general public that
the goals sought cannot be achieved overnight, but are attainable
gradually. He plans to continue his travels in view of the increasing
likelihood of Diet dissolution.

MORALIDUN OF CONVERSATION
SUHJT: Comments of r. Matsumoto on the Current Political Situation.
PARTICIPATS:
Mr. MTSUiOTo Takizo, former Parliamentary Vice Minister
of Foreign Affeirs in the Katayama Cabinet and now
Chairman of the Policy Committee of the People's Coopera-
tive Party.
Mr. W. Henry Lawrence, Jr.
Mr. Yatsumoto stated that recently Dr. ASHIDA Hitoshi, the Prime
Minister, requested thet he inquire of r. YIKI Takeo, President of
the People's Cooperetive Party, whether the latter would be agreeable
to a merger with the Democratie Party. Er. Matsumoto thinks that
Dr. Ashida is seriously worried about the instability of the present
political situation and considers such a merger would have a stabilizing
influence upon the Democratic Party. Mr. Matsumoto pointed out that
the Taiyokai faction of the Democratic Farty (some 30 members) has
been flirting with the Democratic Liheral Party. He seid he is convinced
that Dr. ashida believes this f ction can be held within the party if
the Democratic Party were strengthened by a merger with the People's
Cooperutive Party.
Ir. Miki, eccording to Yr. Matsumoto, would not think of merging
with the Democratic Party as lone as the Taiyokai fuction is a part
of it. Mr. Matsumoto st ted that Nr. Miki, however, came out with a
statement on July 5, 1948 advocating the formation of a new center
party. On receiving news of this, Dr. Ashide indicated hearty endorse-
ment.
Mr. Hatsumoto seid that he expected an extreordinary session of
the Liet in September even though the Social Democrats are advocating
a special session for late July to consider the question of suspension
of interest on war bonds which was shelved at t e Liet Session just
completed. uring the September session, Mr. Matsumoto expects that
either the cabinet will have to resign or t he Diet be dissolved. Mean-
while, Dr. ashida is expected to put off the session as long as possible
and to make strenuous efforts to consolidate the strength of the Govern-
ment Parties as well as to cooperate in the formation of a new party.
Mr. Matsumoto appeared convineed that Dr. Ashida would prefer dissolution
of t he Liet to formetion of a new cabinet by the Democratic Liberal Party.
Mr. Matsumoto

Mr. Matsumoto stressed that Diet members sense the discontent of the
general public and, therefore, despite the risk of losing their seats
are becoming more and more in favor of a general election rather than
resignation of the present cabinet and formation of a new one.
Mr. Matsumoto stated that Mr. NISHIO Suehiro's position of Deputy
Prime Minister, from which he has just resigned following the revelation
before the Illegal Property Transaction Committee, of the receipt and
distribution of ¥5o0,0oo from building contractors, will not be filled.
Dr. Ashida, according to Mr. Matsumoto, expects that Mr. Nishio will be
cleared by the court. If this verdict transpires, Dr. Ashida plans to
have Mr. Nishio return to the cabinet in the same position he formerly
occupied.
Mr. Matsumoto feels thet Mr. NARAyASHI Wataru, a former State
Minister and member of the Democratic Party, who has returned to the
political scene after having been exempted from application of the
purge provisions, is biding his time. Mr. Narahashi does not wish to
become too closely identified with the present sctivities of the
Democratic Party, but prefers to remain in the background until he
considers the time opportune to accept a high position in the party
should Dr. Ashida resign or not be reelected as President at the next
election of party leaders or in a new center party should one be formed.
Mr. Matsumoto expects Mr. Narahashi will emerge gradually as one of the
leading forces in Japanese politics.
Henry Lawenee, Jr.

Osaka riots in April 1948. The trials were held before a United
States Military Commission in hobe, two United States Army Provost

T
only four were found not guilty.
Also enclosed is a copy dated July 7, 1948 of the review by the
CLA
Staff Judge Advocate of the United States Eighth Army of the trial
D
before a United States Military Commission in Kobe of eight Koreans
and one Japanese. This was considered the most important of the
prosecutions made as a result of the April riots. Seven of those
tried were sentenced to confinement for ten years or more and two
were acquitted. The review by the Assistant Staff Judge Advocate
is confined to a suanary of the evidence presented and to a tech-
nical consideration of the leral standard of proof required both to
conform with the specifications and to sustain a conviction of
riot; the review concludes that riot was clearly proved but that,
because this was not a case of riot in its most serious aspects,
CSA

of sentences is recomamended. The opinion of the Staf Judge Advo-
cate emphasizes the seriousness of the assault by the rioters on
United States military personnel and recoanends that the sentences
not be reduced.

UNITLD STATES OF AMEtICA VS KIM DAI SAM et al
Review of the Staff Judge Advocate
1. The attached record of trial of No. 1 Kim Dai Sam, No. 2
Kim Yong Ho, No. 3 Ryo Min Seo, No. 4 Kim Ko Hong, No. 5 Chang Chisco,
No. 6 Kazutomo Horikawa, No. 7 Cha Yong Seok, No. 8 Shin Ki Shik and
No. 9 Kim Chang Shik, tried at Kobe, Honshu, Japan, from 20 May 1948
to 30 June 1948, before a Military Commission appointed by paragraph
1, Special Orders No. 103, this headquarters, 6 May 1948, as amended
by paragraph 1, Special Orders No. 121, this headquarters, 27 May
1948, having been referred to the Staff Judge Advocate, this review
thereof is submitted to the Conmanding General.
2. Personal Data Concernin: the Accused:
Very little personal data concerning the accused was de-
veloped prior to or durin: the course of this trial. All of the
accused are korean nationals with the exception of No. 6, Kazutomo
Horikawa, who is Japanese. They all appear to be responsible persons
with dependents either in Japan or Rorea. ven the youngest, No. 3
Ryo Min Seo, who is only 23 years of age, is an educated man who was
employed as a teacher in the Sanda Korean Primary School. The others
held such responsible positions as, No. 1 xecutive of Korean League
and reporter on Kaiho Newspaper, No. 2 Dressmaker and Secretary of
Korean Association, No. 4 Secretary of the Democratic Youth League,
No. 5 Principal of the Nishikobe Korean Primary School, No. 6 Member
of the Municipal Assenbly of Kobe, No. 8 Textile employee, No. 9
Clerk in offices of Democratic Youth League. It will be noted that
the accused were closely connected with the Korean nationalists move-
ment and were persons of considerable influence and leadership.
Horikawa was a member of the Municipal Assembly of Kobe and an of-
ficial in the Coamunist Farty of that prefecture. He had no particu-
lar reason to be connected with this disturbance in an official
capacity but appeared to be present voluntarily as a representative
of his party. It does not appear how long the various accused have
been resident in Japan but such information is of no importance in
view of the fact that the commission did not adjudge deportation as
part of the sentence awarded.

4. Insanity of Accused:
It does not appear from any evidence before the Commission
or in the opinion of the investigating officer that the accused were
insane or otherwise inconpetent at the time of the trial or at the
time of the alleged commission of the offense. No question was
raised of any insanity and in the absence of such question, the
accused are preswned to be sane (04 1928, par 112a).

6. Comment:
a. In view of the meager identification of Accused No. 4,
Kim Ko Hong, and No. 7, Cha Yong Seok, the comnission justifiably
rendered a finding of not guilty as to these accused of all speci-
fications and the charge. Only one witness testified that he
"thought" No. 4 was present during the negotiations in the Governor's
office on the 24th of April (R 470). Accused No. 7 took the stand
and established the unrefuted alibi that he was at work at his shop
the entire day of the 24th of April, that he had nothing to do with
and knew nothin of the riot.
There is evidence in this case to establish by an over-
whelming preponderance an unlawful assembly to the terror of the
populace as well as the other illegal acts growing out of this cir-
cumstance and charged in specifications 2 through 6. So thorough is
the proof of all factual allegations as to make further discussion
in this regard unnecessary. It renains for the record to contain
identification of each accused and his connection with the riot and
other illegal acts as alleged. This also is accomplished so thorough-
ly and by so many witnesses as not to require specific reference in
this review. It is of importance, however, since this is fundamental-
ly a case of riot and the accused were brought before the commissions
for trial as leaders, that the record should contain evidence estab-
lishing these accused as positive participants and active instigators
of uncontrolable violence. There is such evidence preponderantly
established which, in part and in sunnary, is as follows:

b. There is no coubt that the coinission having been appointed
by the Commanding General, Lighth Army, was properly constituted
under the authority of 1etter, GH, 0Ar, 19 February 1946, "Estab-
lishment of Military Uccu ational Courts," as amended by letter, GHQ,
SCAP, 19 Septenber 1946, "Amendments to xercise of Civil and Criminal
Jurisdiction." The persons charged were properly before the commis-
sion for trial and the subject matter of trial on the surface falls
within the definition of acts overtly prejudicial to the Occupation
and its security. The court properly overruled the pleas to the
jurisdiction (R 27).
c. The cuestion arises hether specifications 2 through 6 do
not, in whole or in part, allege offenses that are lesser included
of specification 1, such as to represent a multiplicity of charges,
since specification 1 al leges enerally the offense of riot. Are not
these other specifications specific descriptions of acts which only
evidenced the riot charged in specitication 1, and as such should be
simply alleged as part of this specification? Two diametrically
opposite positions may be argued in this regard: First, it may be
said that the enphasis in an allegation of riot is upon the unlawful
assembly to the terror of the populace. There is therefore no reason
why these separate acts of violence, occurring as they did away from
the street scene or the eneral scene of riot, may not be separately
charged. They were separately committed, distinguishable by nature
and necessary to properly appraise the accused and the court of this
incident. Second, it may be said that specifications 2 through 6
are simply a recital of facts which describe the riot scene. As such
they should have been included in specification 1. This second
position is undoubtedly the more tenable legal approach. Specifi-
cations 2 through 6 allege such offenses as unlawful entry, assault,
wrongful detention. There is onl/ one way to prove such separate
al legations and that is by proving the corpus delicti and connecting
the various accused with the offense. This the prosecution has not
done. Instead, the prosecution has progressed on the theory that all
principals to a riot are fuilty of all acts of lawlessness committed.
But this could only be so ir such acts are charged as a part of and
indeed, define the riot. To find the accused guilty of an assault,
charged alone in a separate specification, it must be shown that the
accused himself connitted assault, not that the accused is guilty be-
cause he was a principal to a riot charged in another specification.
What would happen to the assault under this theory if the riot speci-
fication failed in proof?
However, the nature of this case is not such as to com-
pel answer to this problem. It is well settled that even where there
has
RESTRICTED

=== Page 234 === (confidence 0.99)
Enclosure No. 2 to Tokyo's
No. 512, August 12, 1948.
- 9 -
has been an unnecessary multiplication of charges, this is not pref-
udicial when the sent ence imposed is within the limit for any one of
the specifications (Bul1 JAG, 1944, p. 234). There are no maximum
sentences in this case and a review of the sentences awarded does
not indicate that the multiplicity affected the outcome of trial, for
the same sent ences might well have been awarded for any one of the
specifications alleged.
d. The accused take the position in this case that they were
part of a grouppursuing a lawful purpose, that they progressed toward
the accomplishment of this purpose and that it simply "got out of
hand." The facts and the law refute such a position. The established
proof that an uncontrolled mob of Koreans set out on the illegal mis-
sion of enforcing their will on the government, irrespective of the
means that had to be employed, cannot be avoided. In its inception,
the concerted will of this group was illegal. They had the intent
mutually to assist one against anyone who should oppose them. A
proper defense in this case would be proof that the individual, if
present, was engaged in suppressing participants, instead the evidence
supports the contrary, that the accused were actually the ringleaders
and took an active part in the lawlessness and acts of violence. Nor
would it be necessary to extend the definition of the law this far
in order to find the accused guilty as charged. As a general rule,
where "their presence is intentional, and where it tends to the en-
couragement of the rioters," it may be prima facie inferred that they
are participants, each chargeable with responsibility for the acts
of the others (22 C.J.S., Criminal Law, Par 87a; U.S. v. Kan, Hea
Chang, et al, Mil Comm Chinju Korea, 11-18 Feb 47). Eminently is
this the case where police officers arrive and demand that those
present give assi stance in suppressing the difficulty. From that
point on there can be, "deliberately remaining, no neutrals."
(wharton's Criminal Law, Vo1 2, Sec 1865, 12th d)
e. The charge in this case alleges acts "prejudicial to the
security" and "the objectives" of the Occupation Forces. There is no
doubt but that such a charge is one of which a duly appointed commis-
sion may properly take jurisdiction. It may be said that such a
charge should include a referece to the particular directive defin-
ing such acts as offenses as, indeed, it is always desirable to have
pleading as conplete as possible. Certain jurisdictional qualifica-
tions may al so be indicat ed in this way. Any such objection, however,
challenges the tora and not the legality of this charge.
Of the six specifications alleged, can it be said that they
appraise the accused, on the surface, of acts prejudicial to the
security and objectives of the occupation? The answer to this ques-
tion must undoubtedly be in the affirmative. The Japanese Govern-
ment, except where it has been limited by directives from SCAP, is
ordered to exercise jurisdiction over domestie disturbance and civil
police. Interference in this authority is manifestly an interference
with: the objectives of the Occupation.
Specification 2 is a possible exception which, stripped of
descriptive matter, alleges an assault and unlawful entry. The
proven facts of this case, however, unquestionably show the underlying
connection of the assault and unlawful entry with the illegal purposes
behind the riot. Thus, they may be said to fall within the general
definition of prejudicial acts described by the charge.

f. It appears that due to extreme illness, the accused No. 6,
Horikawa, was absent repeatedly throughout the trial (R 125). The
commission proceeded with the trial in his absence to his convic-
tion and sentence along with the other accused. The president
repeatedly asked the defense counsel whether or not this accused
was being kept up to date and the accused was brought in before the
findings and sentence were announced. The accused is required to
be present in court throughout the entire proceeding (par 55, MC,
1928). However, in the absence of procedure so prejudicial as to
be shocking to the conscience, this must be held sufficient as an
expediency under paragraph 4d, 1etter GHQ, SCAP, 19 February 1946,
"Establishment of Military Occupation Courts." Under this provision
the commission has authority to prescribe such rules of procedure
as are necessary for the expeditious handling of the case.
E. Under paragraph 5, 1etter GHQ, CAP 19 February 1946, the
accused are entitled to a copy of the charges before trial and are
entitled to have present at the trial both counsel and interpreter.
It is thus the obvious intention of this letter that the accused
should have a couy of the charges that would be intelligible to the
accused, that is, a copy in some language understood by the accused.
The accused were originally served with a copy of the charge and
specifications in unglish, contrary to this provision (R 24). How-
ever, it cannot be said that the accused were thus prejudiced. No
objection was made by the defense, the president ordered the charge
and specifications served in Japanese (a 25) and indeed the whole
record translated in open court for the benefit of the accused.
There were no motions for continuance or requests by the defense
fortime in which to prepare the defense that were not reasonably
granted. The entire record indicates that the accused were well pre-
pared. The trial lasted for 40 days. There is no doubt but that
the accused were given adequate notice.
h. The record in this case is cluttered with inconsequential
trivia, immaterial argument hetween counsel and unnecessary instruc-
tions from the court. For example, several pages of the record are
filled with discussion between counsel and the court, in which the
prosecution attempted to ret what anounted to an order of the court
permitting the taking of a deposition (R 194); at page 31, defense
requested an open discussion of the prosecution's view of the case;
definitions purportin to have legal consequence were read from
Webster's Dictionary (a 33); and directive letters to the trial
judge advocate and jurisdictional directives from SCAP were read in-
to the record (i 8-l0). The nost that can be said, however, is that
a voluminous and tangled record has been submitted which although
procedurally confused, has not prejudiced the accused.
Further, there are many exaaples where the commission, out
of an attitude of extreme fairness, went to great trouble, at the ex-
pense of time and effort to grant the slightest request of the accused
(i 21, 26, 38, 68). without reservation it nay be said that the ac-
cused received a fair and impartial trial, were granted rights beyond
the legal requirements and were aost ably defended by both civilian
and appointed defense counsel.
i. In concluding this comnent, a review of the record in this
case indicates that, except for those procedural matters expressly
excepted

excepted by letter GH2, SCAP, 19 February 1946 and the question
raised in paragraph f above, this case could be reviewed upon the
standards of procedure indicated in the United States Army MCM, 1928
and held legally sufficient thereunder. It may also be noted that
only once was it necessary to resort to paragraph 4d, letter GHQ,
CAP, 19 February 1946, wherein the commission is authorized to
alter the formal procedure of trial in order to justify procedural
action of tle commission in the trial of this case.
7. lenency: Counsels for the accused, members of their
families and interested persons have submitted petitions for clemency
on their tehalf. Said petitions have been examined and attached to
the record.
There is some uestion whether the facts of this case justi-
fy the sentences imposed. Although an unmistakable case of riot has
been proved, the facts renain that it is minimized by: A failing in
proof to show physical injury to anyone, the presence of dangerous
weapons, there was no great terror among the people to cause anyone
to flee from the scene, actual strikin: or threat beyond simple
assault and intimidation. There is mitigation in the fact that this
occurrence arises out of prolonged racial difficulty and a desire of
the Koreans simply to be left alone. The inception of the difficulty
was in positive action taken by the Japanese, not the Koreans. A
study of the accused themselves indicates that they are not a criminal
type, they are school teachers and leaders among their people. Al-
though the acts do chsrge offenses prejudicial to the security and
objectives of the Occupation, they are not directly so. There was
an obvious belief on the part of all that they were simply solving a
Korean-Japanese problem, lon festered by o pression of a minority
group. Only the ccused Horikawa indicated a premeditated intent
distinuishable from the aoove. He was not a art of the movement
and simply injected hinself into it for whatever personal advantage
he night zet or whatever enbarrassnent he mi ht cause the Japanese
Government. His oifense, therefore, is actually nore serious than
that of the others.
Chapter VI11, Japanese Jode, 1907, as amended, carries a
maximum sentence of 10 years for t e ringleaders of a riot. Assault
with the intent to comait a felony carries a maximum sentence of 10
years confinement in the i., 1929. This case does not contemplate
riot in its most serious aspects ari consequently punishable in the
maximum anounts. It is therefore reconmended that the sentences be
reduced to one-half that awarded in each case with the exception of
Horikawa whose sentence should not be reduced below that approved
for any of the other accused.

The comnission was properly constituted.
b.
It had jurisdiction of the persons and offenses.
C.
The evidence supports the findings of guilty.
d.
The record contains no errors injuriously affect-
ing the substantial rights of the accused.
e.
The sentences are legal.

I concur in principle. retitions for clemency have been fully
considered.
Pleading the separate acts in separate specifications was correct
as it avoided multifariousness and facilitated a defense by accused
as to the matters against which they had proof. Since it was estab-
lished in the instances where ruilt was adjudged that the accused
concerned were participants either actively or by aiding and abetting
by word and act as accessories (hence principals), the corpus delicti
was proved (50 Bit 3 220J rim Law 157).
Chang Chisco and the others sought and accepted leadership in the
negotiations. They led a crowd which some of its leaders had whipped
up into fury by oratory and en hasizing fancied wrongs up to the
vicinity of the object of its wrath, the Governor. Can it be said
that he who advances the unpowder to a spark shall not be held for
the consequences? The law holds one for the reasonable results of
his actions. These leaders are not above the law.
The statements in the foregoing review concerning reduction of
sentences are not concurred in. The fact that the culprits were in-
telligent persons militates against them. They knew that civiliza-
tion rests upon law, order, and peaceful change and correction of
alleged abuses by lawful and constitutional means not upon riot and
illegal force. They knew that the civilized nations are building
democracy in Japan by use of the carefully supervised Japanese in-
digenous governnental structure. When Occupation Force authorities
appeared on the scene, in uniforn, they violated that uniform, by
violence frustr: ted the legal lesires of its wearers and personally
assaulted them. in the only other instance of this type, an early
case involvin: Japanese accused and evidencing much less resistance
to Occupation authority, occurring near Tokyo, a sentence of life
imprisonment for the ringleader and twenty years' confinement at hard
labor for the other participants was approved. Approval of the
sentences as adjudged by the commission is recomnended.

COMIENTS ON MEMORANDUM CONCERNING THE PURGE OF ISHIBASHI TANZAN
The information conoerning the purge of ISHIBASHI Tanzan contained
in the memorandum forwarded by Mr. liarry F. Kern is in general confirmed
by information available from other sources, including the off-the-
à
record statements of former SCAP officials. Some of the details of the
case were not previously known to DRF, e.g., Ishibashi's attempt to get
an interview with General Whitney and the petitions filed by prominent
individuals in behalf of Ishibashi. The conclusions stated by the au-
thor of the memorandum (pages V and VI) are in most instances substan-
tially accurate. In connection with the conclusion stated in Item a,
p. V, it might be noted that it is certainly well known in Japan, at
least among the politically informed groups, that General Headquarters
intervened to order the Japanese screening comnittee to purge Ishibashi
after he had previously been clesred by the committee. On the other
hand, the conclusion stated in  tem c, p. V. seems to be overstated, ac-
cording to information available here.
DRF has never reviewed the contents of the Oriental Economist
during the prewar period in order to determine whether the editorial
opinions expressed therein were of a militaristic or anti-American
character. DRF is, theretore, not in a position at this time to judge
whether the SJAP interpretation of the editorial character of this
nagazine is correct. Regardless of whether or not the SCAP position
that Ishivashi should be purged on the basis of his editorship of the
Oriental Eeonomist can be justified, there is evidence that the finan-
cial policies pursued by Ishibashi, while he was Finance inister in
RESTRICTED
7

=== Page 240 === (confidence 0.99)
RESTRICTED
2
tne Yoshida Cabinet, were disapproved by headquarters officials.
It should be noted that the purge was instituted by a SCAP direo-
tive issued on January 4, 1946 pursuant to the statement in the Potsdam
Declaration that reads: "There must be eliminated for all time the au-
thority and influence of those who have deceived and misled the people
of Japan into embarking on world conquest...." By the directive,
and Japanese ordinances issued subsequent thereto, this provision of
the Potsdam Declaration was broadly interpreted. SCAP has reviendthe
actions of the Japanese purge committees and has on other occasions
intervened to order the purge of individuals previously cleared by the
Japanese committees. SCAP supervision of the operation of the purge is
clearly within the field of implenentation of policy that SCAP has main-
tained is its exclusive jurisdiction, ed therefore neither the US Govern-
ment nor the FEC has attempted to interfere.

Subject: Japanese Police Ban on Parades and Demonstrations in Osaka.
The Acting Political Adviser has the honor to refer to this
Mission's despatch No. 527 of August 17, 1948 forwarding e copy
of a letter from Major General A. P. Kislenko, Acting Soviet Member,
Allied Council for Japan, to General of the Army Douglas MacArthur,
and to enclose a copy of a press release of August 12, 1948 from
General Headquarters, Far East Command, concerning General Kislenko's
demand that a regulation concerning meetings and demonstrations
issued by the Osaka Police Department on July 13, 1948 be cancelled.
In his letter, General Kislenko claimed this regulation was another
step in the Occupation's program to suppress activities of labor
unions, and in essence grants the police the right to prohibit any
meeting or demonstration or arrest any participants in these activities
and their leaders.
In the press release, the Commanding General of I Corps, Major
General Joseph M. Swing, denied the issuance of a directive by the
Provost Marshal of the 25th Infantry Division, on which General Kislenko
had claimed the police regulation was based. General Swing stated
that the police had acted on an informel memorandum from the Provost
Marshal prepared when the Japanese police sought his advice, and that
parts of the instructions issued by the Japanese police which General
Swing found to interfere unduly with the rights of assembly were
reseinded on his orders.
CS
Furthermore, Generel Swing declared that on its own initiative
NV
the Osaka City Assembly passed an ordinance on the same subject, but
since parts of it appeared to violate the civil liberties of the
Japanese people he directed that the ordinance be held in abeyance
until the next meeting of the assembly (about September 1). The
Public Safety Committee of Osaka met on August 13, in an emergency
session, and agreed immediately to suspend the operation of the ordinance
and to subject demonstrations and public gatherings only to the restriction
promulgated on December 26, 1946 which requires advance notice of five
days. The Osaka Municipal Assembly is expected to hold an urgent session
to act formally in this matter.
While the actions of the Occupation authorities in Osaka clearly
inaicate an alertness to the need for protecting the civil liberties
of the Japanese people, the issuance of an ordinance after receipt of an
informal memorandum from the local Occupation authorities gave General
Kislenko a pretext sufficient for use to attack the labor policies
advocated by this Headquarters. General Kislenko ignored the subsequent
steps taken by General Swing to rescind any orders which might be conatrued
as infringements of civil liberties.

12 August 1948
WITH THE EIGHTH ARY IN KYOTO--In regard to a statement appearing
in the Nippon Times of Thursday, August 12, 194e, to the effect that
last week 25th Division officers denied they had ever instructed
Japanese police to issue restrictions on public meetings, the Command-
ing General of I Corps, Maj. Gen Toseph M. Swing, issued the following
amplifying statement today:
"To prevent the recurrence of riots similar to those in
the Osaka-Kobe aree on the 23d and 24th of April, the Japanese
police of Osaka City, when informed thai. unauthorized parades
and demonstrations were being planned on the 13th and 15th of
July, sought the advice of the tactical troops es to the manner
in which to preserve order. Acting on an informal memorandum
prepared by the Provost Mershal, 25th Division, which indicated
measures taken under similar circumstances in the United States,
the Japenese police about July l2th issued general instructions
on parades, demonstrations and other activities involving public
safety and tra fic congestion. Such parts of those instructions
which might be construed as interferring unduly with the right
of assembly were rescinded promptly by my orders.
"Shortly thereafter the Osaka City Assembly on its own
initietive passed an ordinance on the same subject. Some
provisions of this ordinance I considered violated Scapin 93,
which granted civil liberties to the Japanese people. Accordingly
on August 2d, I directed that implementation of this ordinance
be held in abeyance pending further consideration of its provisions
at the next regular meeting of the Osaka City Assembly about the
lst of September".

Dear Butterworth,
Japanese affairs have been arousing more interest
in Britain recently than has been the case during the
past few months, largely because of the discussion in
Japan and elsewhere of the MacArthur-Ashida prohibition
of strikes and collective bargaining by civil servants
and government employees. This interest is only natural
in a country which has a Labor (Socialist) government
and a strong trade union movement.
There were several news despatches from Tokyo
published in local newspapers, describing the moves
taken by General MacArthur and Premier Ashida to prevent
a paralyzing general strike of government workers. Both
894.00
the Times and the Manchester Guardian also published
reasonably full accounts of the debate in the Allied
Council for Japan on the subject. The Economist of
August 28 published a short article on the subject,
describing the plight of the government workers in
Japan, whose salaries have not nearly kept pace with
the rising cost of living, ana the steps leading to
Ashida's Cabinet Ordinance of July 3l. The article was
not critical and concluded on the following note: "Against
6
this reproach (the resination of Killen) General MacArthur
relies on a supra-mundane authority; he triumphantly
quotes the late President Roosevelt as saying that a
力
strike by government employees is 'unthinkable and in-
tolerable'".
8
The Times on September 3 contained an editorial
which was sympathetic to General MacArthur but rather
critical of the Japanese Government and the remnants of
the Zaibatsu. After rehearsing the general history of
the growth of the trade union movement since the close
of World War II and the tendency of unions of government
workers/
William W. Butterworth, Jr., Esquire,
Director of Office of Far Eastern Affairs,
Department of State,
Washington, D.0.

=== Page 262 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL
-2-
workers to fall into the hands of Communists, the
editorial stated: "General MacArthur quite properly
pointed out, in a letter to the Japanese Government,
that there was an important distinction to be drawn
between Government officials on the one hand and em-
ployees in State enterprises on the other . . . . The
Japanese Government . . . . seized the opportunity
presented by the MacArthur letter to strike a heavy
blow at the growth of trade unionism. Collective bar-
gaining was forbidden not only to Government officials
but also to all workers in the many State-controlled
industries. . . . The power of the Zaibatsu over the
politicians and the press is still so extensive that
only General MacArthur now stands between the trade
unions and the threat of virtual suppression which hangs
over them." The editorial continued by discussing the
follies of the Japanese labor leaders and the intrigues
of the Communists, and stated: "his (General MacArthur's
policy of rebuilding the economy of Japan upon free
competition, individual enterprise, small businesses, and
liberation from the stranglehold of the Zaibatsu is
hindered, not helped, by attempts on the part of trade
union officials to subvert the ordinary machinery of
administration by using their power to bring the Gov-
ernment to a standstill."
I took advantage of an opportunity to discuss this
matter of the right of government employees to strike
with MacDermot. He said that the position of the Foreign
Office continued to be that already conveyed to the
Department (Circular Airgram of August 24, 8:50 a.m.).
He said that public servants in Britain are not for-
bidden to strike, but that adequate measures are pro-
vided for their protection. For example, they are not
required, as in Japan, to petition their particular
department for relief but are permitted to submit their
grievances to an impartial tribunal. He thought that
something like this might be worked out in Japan and
hoped that SCAP would pay some attention to the little
talk of the Commonwealth Representative at the Allied
Council meeting of August 28, at which Mr. Patrick Shaw
had offered the long experiences of the British Common-
wealth in the field of labor relations for the benefit
of the Jananese Government. He said that the Foreign
Office thought that Shaw had said exactly the right
thing.
I remarked/

=== Page 263 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL
-3-
I remarked that the Soviet representative in Tokyo
had already brought the whole question before the
Allied Council and mentioned the possibility that the
Soviet representative on the FEC might introduce a
resolution into that body with the purpose of censoring,
directly or indirectly, General MacArthur for the part
he played in suppressing the government workers of
Japan. MacDermot said most emphatically that there
must be no censoring or criticism of MacArthur under
any circumstances; that the UK would absolutely oppose
any such idea. He said that the Cabinet Ordinance in
question is now being redrafted before presentation
to the Diet, and that we should take advantage of the
delay to have informal talks on the matter. If the
Soviets introduce a resolution in the FEC, we should
stall for time, in the hope that the redraft of the
Ordinance as introduced into the Diet will be acceptable.
It would be most unfortunate if there should be acri-
monious discussion of the matter in the FEC, as such
discussions always become public sooner or later. It
is essential, said MacDermot, that we suppress criticism
of MacArthur.
Miscellansous Comment. On September 2 the Times
carried a news despatch from Tokyo stating that Dr.
Justin Williams, head of the Parliamentary and Political
Division of the Government Section of SCAP, had ad-
vocated at a press conference the establishment in
Japan of a committee similar to the U.S. House Com-
mittee on Un-American Activities, for the purpose of
investigating "un-Japanese activities" - presumably
meaning Communist activities. In commenting upon this
proposal, the Manchester Guardian on September 3 had
this to say: "On Wednesday General MacArthur announced
a new recruit: Japan is becoming 'a bastion to the
democratic concept.'. . . But for sheer fantasy Dr.
Williams, one of General MacArthur's chief political
advisers, has even his master beat. Failing completely
to realize how ridiculous the House Committee on Un-
American Activities has made his own country look in
foreign eyes, he has proposed that the Tokyo Diet should
set up, with full publicity, a Committee on Un-Japanese
Activities. The Communists, whose party was legalized
in order to make Japan more democratic, are now to be
hunted in order to make her more Japanese, and when
one thinks what the main Japanese 'activity' has been
during the last seventeen years it scunds more than a
little odd."
Tha Economist/

=== Page 264 === (confidence 0.99)
CONFIDENTIAL
-4-
The Economist of September 4 published a carefully-
prepared article by an anonymous writer (I believe it
was by a Miss Byrd, an Amerioan member of the staff of
the Economist, who sometimes calls at the Embassy to
read background material), entitled "Prospects of
Japanese Recovery." The article described the diffi-
culties experienced by Japan in endeavors to restore the
pre-war pattern of trade; the attempts made by SCAP to
have the Japanese balance their budget (attempts which
were thwarted: "In part this is due to high occupation
costs . . . and in part it is the result of Japanese
flaccidity"); the attempts now being made to pare down
reparations; the slowing down of the dissolution of the
Zaibatsu in order to increase production; the failure
of Congress to provide adequate funds for rehabilitation
of Japanese industry; the need for private foreign
investment in Japan; the bilateral trade agreements
being concluded between Japan and Far Eastern countries;
and the need for a single exchange rate for the yen
instead of the multiple rates now existing. The article
concluded: "The immediate economic prospect for Japan
does not make a cheerful picture. Japanese political
leaders will have to convince the population that for
some time to come their standard of living is likely to
be much lower than before the war. Indeed, if the
Japanese themselves were to bear the full economic
consequences of the war, there wculd be mass starvation
in the cities. Something le ss than this austerity will
be called for. But, even so, there can only be a real
break in the present impasse when Japan produces a
government prepared to face the facts - and the unpop-
ularity."
Sincerely yours,
Erle R. Dickover

Dear Mr. Karn:
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter of 6 August 1948
inclosing a photostat of a document written by Mr. Tansan Ishibashi,
in which he argues that his purge while holding the office of Minis-
ter of Finance in the Yoshida government was unjust.
The mtter of Tanzan Ishibashi has heretofore been called to the
attention of the Department of the Army and an investigation and re-
port has been received from General Headquarters Far East Command.
Portions of this report are quoted below for your information:
"The action taken by the Japanese Government in
screening Ishibashi, Tanzan, has been reviewed and
disapproved. Ishibashi, Minister of Finance, is to
be removed from public office and excluded from pub-
Lic service as a Category G, Appendix A, SCAPIN 550.
"As editor and president of the Oriental Economist,
he (Ishibashi) was responsible for the policies of that
publication which supported military and economic im-
perialiem in Asia, advocated Japan's adherence to the
Axis, fostered belief in the inevitability of war with
the Westsrn Powers, justified suppression of trade union-
iam, and urged imposition of totalitarian controls over
the Japanese people. * * * The supporters of Tanzan
Ishibashi are those who unmindful of the immense sacri-
fice of human and material resources occasioned by the
war, now seek insofar as possible to protect the ald
order of Japan and its institutions and influences which
share war responsibility, and whose suppression is not
only required by basic Allied policy but is a mandatory
requisite to the opportunity for future democratic growth.
259

=== Page 267 === (confidence 0.99)
"Tansan Ishibashi's voiee and pen are among
these which bear predominant responsibility for shap-
ing the Japanese mental processes toward war of con-
quest, the suppression of human rights among the
Japanese msses, and the welding of Japanese eoonomy
into the close association with the military whick
ultimately prosecuted the war. The pretense of his
friendship for the United States finds clear refutation
in his advocacy of war against the United States many
months prior to Pearl Harbor; his liberalism, in his
extolling of the virtues of Hitler and the Nazi philoso-
phy, his advocacy of a totalitarian state in peace as
in war and his hailing of the suppression of trade
unioniam; his pacifism, in his open support of militar-
istic moves and objectives and his constant plea for
expanded conquest and military s upport of Germany and
Italy against the Western Powers — all long before
the attack on Pearl Harbor or the acute deterioration
of Japanese-American relations."
While every effort has been made by General Headquarters, SCAp to use
the machinery of the Japanese Government in carrying out the direct re-
quirements of the Potsdam Declaration, that Headquarters has not hesitated
to exert pressure in cases where it appeared that the Japanese were either
unable or umwilling to purge individuals clearly falling within the soope
of the purge directive.
You are possibly aware that the termination of the purge activities
of General Headquarters, SCAP was announced in a press release from that
Headquarters on 22 June 19L8.

imately thirty minutes late and during this interval General Chang and .I
conversed in Japanese. During this part of the conversation, General Chang
expressed his great appreciation to me for the arrangements which had been
made for him to interview many officers of General Headquarters, Japanese
officials and others, and for the special airplane which had been placed
at his disposal for his trip to Hiroshima and Osaka. He said that the
local military commanders at Hiroshima, Osaka, Kobe and Kyoto had been
extremely kind in affording all desired facilities to him and in making
possible numerous interviews with local Occupation and Japanese officials.
General Chan: said that he has obtained considerable detailed know-
ledge regarding the Occupation and while he does not consider everything
to be perfect, on balance he feels that the Occupation is an unparalleled
success.
In summing up his impressions regarding the political situation in
Japan General Chan said that he is satisfied with the great advances
which have been made in the formation of political parties along democratic
lines and which are led by fairly good leaders. On the other hand, however,
he is somewhat disturbed by the present political unrest which, in his
opinion, is largely ccasioned by pressure from the extreme right and left
upon the middle-of-the-road government presently in power. He wondered
whether it would not be possible for SCAP to give greater support to middle-
of-the-road parties by selecting competent leaders and by encouraging the
Japanese people to support these leaders. I replied that in my opinion
SCAP would be ill-advised to inject himself into Japanese internal politics,
as to do so would, in effect, amount to a negation of a proper democratic.
process. In other words, I added, if General liacArthur were to show favor to
certain individuals he would merely be substituting himself for the former
cliques which in the past ruled and controlled Japanese politics. I said that
in my opinion it is wiser to allow the Japanese to select their own leaders
and that in time, as experience is gained, appropriate leaders would come to
the fore.
CONFIDENTIAL
In reply

=== Page 272 === (confidence 0.99)
Encl. to
Tokyo's 600
September 13,1948
-2-
CONFIDENTIAL
In reply to a question which I asked concerning General Chang's im-
pressions regarding the communist situation in Japan, he stated that in
his opinion the Japanese are fortunate in not having Chinese communists
as a political factor in Japan. He referred to the influence of Chinese
communists in other Asiatic countries, particularly in southeast Asia,
and said that at least the Japanese communists are not directly influenced
or controlled by their Chinese counterparts. On the other hand, he is
certain that the Japanese communists are largely directed and influenced
by Soviet communists centered at Vladivostok---he said that all communists
in the Far East look to Vladivostok as the "center of the Far East".
General Chang voiced the opinion that SCAP should exercise greater
pressure against the communist party in Japan and should make a determined
effort to arouse enthusiastic support to an anti-communist campaign in
Japan. (I pointed out that under FEC directives this might be extremely
difficult in view of the underlying spirit of these directives that all
Allied countries should have a part in formulating policies pertaining to
the Occupation of Japan.)
In summing up the Occupation, General Chang said that there has been
so much misinformation and slanted comment concerning American aims and
policies in Japan that it is almost impossible to know exactly what these
aims and policies are. He therefore felt it extremely urgent and necessary
that the United States Government, by public announcement, clarify its
policy not only in Japan but in the Far East as a whole. He said that if
the aim of the United States in the occupation of Japan is to build up a
bastion of defense against Communism then he would say that no one has a
right to criticize what is being done. On the other hand if United States
policies are solely to carry out announced directives of the FEC and of the
United States, as well as the Potsdam Declaration and the Terms of Surrender,
considerable clarification is needed in order to still criticism and to ex-
plain United States intentions.
General Chang asked what I thought of the possibility of an early Peace
Conference in order to settle the Japanese situation. I told General Chang
that I am not well informed on this subject and of course could only give my
personal opinion, but that it would appear to me that several outstanding
problems of major importance, such as reparations and level of industry,
ought to be settled before a Peace Conference is called. I said that it ap
pears to me as unrealistic to think that the mere signin of a Peace Treaty
would automatically cure all outstanding problems, as obviously, unless a
solution is found for the major difficulties which are still outstanding, it
would be hopeless to go into a Peace Conference with the pious wish that
such problems could more readily be solved at the peace table. General Chang
thought for a moment and said that he entirely agrees vith my personal
opinion and felt that his Government should not make the mistake of urging
the convocation of an imnediate Peace Conference. He said that in any event
he feels that the Japanese need more time in order to get their house in order
and properly to digest many of the reforas which, in some cases, have been
forced upon them against their wishes.
CONFIDENTIAL
In conclusion

 NFIDENTIAL
In conclusion General Chang said that he feels certain that he is
now sufficiently well informed regarding the Japanese situation to clarify
many doubts concerning the Occupation and United States policy in Japan
among not only high officials of the Chinese Government, but also among
the Chinese people at large.
W. J. Sebald

Katayama Cabinet, pointed out that, at the time of the

Reasons for Mr. Katayama's Advocating
Diet Dissolution
Mr. Kateyama has been the most out-spoken of any of
the government party heads in favor of dissolution of the
Diet. At first, this position appeared strange since
Mr. Ketayama tends toward the right wing faction of the
Social Democratic Party wnich has indicated a desire to
avoid Diet dissolution as long as possible, while the left
wing faction hes been vociferous in its advocacy of Diet
dissolution. Mr. Miki recently told an officer of this
Mission that, in his opinion, Mr. Katayama advocated Diet
dissolution as & means of holding the Socialist Party's
two factions together. This same analysis of Mr.
Katayame's position is well set forth in the enclosed
editorial from the Nippon Times for September 8, 1948.
It has been learned on reliable authority that Mr.
Katsyama himself read this Nippon Times editorial and
indicated that it was such an accurate anelysis of his
thinking thet he would heve liked to have seen it printed
in all Jepenese newspepers. The editorial points out
that Mr. Katayama believes the early dissolution of the
Diet is the surest means of preserving the present
coalition, which in his opinion is the only practical
government under existing circumstances. The editorial
further states that Mr. Kateyeme's reasoning involves a
desire to prevent a quarrel from breaking up the cosli-
tion between the Democratic Party end the Social
Democratic Perty, e querrel which might be brought on
by the dissatisfaction of the left wing faction of the
latter perty. According to the editorial, Mr. Ketayema
believes thet if the Diet is dissolved before e break-up
occurs, cooperation between the two parties will not be
prevented in the future. In addition, the editorial
declares that Mr. Katayama probably calculates, as do
most other political experts, that e general election
would result in little change in the House of Representa-
tives end therefore that any new coalition formed would
be very similer to the one now in power.
Prime Minister Ashida in July appeered resigned to
the eventual dissolution of the Diet this coming fall,
but, since the July 22 letter of General MacARTHUR
recommending revision of the Netional Public Service Lew,
and developments therefrom, Mr. Ashida has shown
increesing confidence that Diet dissolution is not
imminent. His position, which this Headguarters is
believed to share, is that the expense, uncertainty, and
distraction of an election campaign should under present
circumstances be avoided if possible.

"Approval in Principle" - Resounding Victory
for Right Wing Socialists
Mr. Miki informed an officer of this Mission that
even the left wing faction of the Social Democratic
Party has become less anxious for immediate Diet
dissolution, but to "seve face" all around, the Social
Democratic Party hes "approved in principle" Mr.
Katayama's stand on an early Diet dissolution. In our
opinion this "approval in principle" was a compromise
between the two factions of the party which came about
when the left wing faction agreed to withdraw its
original demend for a wholesale withdrawal of the Social
Democratic members of the Cebinet as a preliminary to
Diet dissolution.
In the Nippon Times editorial of September 17,
several factors are cited as contributing to the sudden
emergence of the right wing faction in the Social
Democratic Perty:
(1) Acquittal of Mr. NISHIO Suehiro
by the Tokyo District Court (this Mission's
Airgram 188 of September 9, 1948).
(2) Expulsion of the extreme left
wing group.
(3) weakening of the left wing faction
by prospects of increased rice ration and
of introduction of foreign capital (coupled
with this is the proposed revision of the
National Public Service Law which would
serve to prevent a concerted labor offensive
against the government).
(4) Disadvantege to the left wing, in
discussion of withdrawal from the Cabinet, in
having in the Cabinet two members who desire
to retein their positions.
It is also of interest that, in this editoriel, the
Socialist agreement to concentrete on policy matters
rether then seek an eerly Diet dissolution is noted as
leaving & wide loop-hole through which the party may
still ask for Diet dissolution et any time. Both right
wing and left wing leaders agreed to withhold final
decision until they have ascerteined how far Prime
Minister Ashida is prepared to go in accepting Social
Democratic policies.
Results of Meeting of Heeds of Government
Parties
On September 9, 1948, ir. Miki volunteered the
information that at & meeting of the three government
party leaders on September 14, e decision similar to
thet of the Social Democratic Ferty's "approval in
principle" of Diet dissolution might be reached In
order to "save face" for Mr. Kateyama, but that no

determination

- 4 -
determination would be made as to the time of dissolution.
According to & press statement made by Mr. Miki following
the meeting of September l4, the question of Diet
dissolution was only considered informally after the three
leaders had agreed on October 1, 1948 as a possible date
for the opening of the extraordinary session of the Diet
for a period of thirty days (from a practical point of
view, Jepanese leaders expect the session to begin about
October 10 and last longer then thirty days). Apparently,
the question of Diet dissolution has become less urgent,
hence, the heads of the three government parties have
felt it unnecessary to reach any formal decision, even a
"face-seving" one.
Conclusion
As we have previously pointed out (this Mission's
despatch No. 514 of August 31, 1948), the Ashida Cabinet
gained & new lease on life as a result of General
MacArthur's July 22 letter recommending revision of the
National Public Service Law. The victory of the right
wing of the Social Democratic Party has further assured
the Cabinet a much needed breathing spell. We find this
outcome desirable in that it is herdly likely that a
dissolution of the Diet and & generel election at this
time would bring about en improvement in the general
situetion which might, in turn, compensate for the
resultant politicel vecuum, uncertainty, and expense
involved. In our opinion, the whole ouestion of Diet
dissolution has been reised by politicians and is not
the result of pressure of popular opinion.

ORADU FO: The ief of Staff.
SUBJACT:
Sentences Jiven to Koreans Involved in Kobe Riots.
Ir. Patrick Shaw, Jhief of the Australian ission, called upon
me on September 23, 1943 for the purp se o1 making an oral represen-
tation on behalf of the Koreans tho were recently tried and sentenced
by a military conmission in Kobe on the charge of acts prejudicial to
the security of the Occupation Forces in Japan and to the objectives
of the Occupation in Jupan.
I. Shaw statei that he has noted and advised his government
that the sentences given to the six Koreans and one Japanese vary from
ten to fifteen years confinement at hard labor. He stated that he has
no interest in the case of the Japanese (sentenced to ten years). On
the ot' er hand, his overmment feuls, in view of the tpe of Korean
individuals involved and the ciremastances surrounding the acts with
wiich they were charged, that tne sentenceo are excessive in contrast
with sentences usually iven in other sourts. He noted particularly
that five of the Koreans received sentences of fifteen years at hard
labor, and one Korean twelve years.
I questioned kr. Jhaw concerin the motives of his representa-
tion and asked whether his otive is olitical. ie replied that the
representation was made on huanitarian rounds, as well as for the
reason that in the opinion of is overnnent, the sentences are
excessive and migt create an imoression aaons Oriental pec ples of
harsh Western justice. He said that e las no criticism whatsoever
concerning the fairness of the trials. He also said that he has
received several petitions frea various korean roups asking for an
amelioration of the sentences, including one from the individuals
themselves. (In this connection, I have also received similar peti-
tions addressed to me as Jhaimian, Allied Jouncil for Japan.)
I told r. shaw that in so far as I lave been able to determine,
the sentences have already been reviewed and ap proved by the Comnanding
General, Cth Anay, and that, under normal procedure, no further review
is possible. I stated, however, that I would invite the attention of
the appropriate authorities to his representation.

HEMDRANDUN OF CONWERSATION
SECRET
September 3, 1948.
Participants:
Sir Alvary D. F. GASCOINE, Hoad
of the United Kingdom Liaison Mission
in Japan.
Hr. W. J. Sobald
Sir Alvary GASCOIGNE called at my office by appointment for the
purpose of conveying to me certain information regarding his recent trip
to London. During his stay at the Foreign Office, Sir Alvary said that
he met with Mr. Bevin upon two occasions and worked very alosely with
Mr. Dening and Mr. MoDermott of the Par Eastern desk.
Sir Alvary said that in general the Japanese situation, which ap-
peared to be going moothly, was relegated to a secondary position by
the Foreign Office in view of the more pressing problems of Europe and
elsewhere. On the other hand, he said that the Foreign Office view re-
garding a Japanese Peace Treaty continues unchanged and that it is hoped
that a peace conference can be convoked as soon as possible. He said that
the British view is that domestio politics in the United States would
probably prealude any possibility of a peace conference being summoned be-
fore next spring, but it is the Foreign Office's hope that a conferance can
be sumoned at that time. When I queried Sir Alvary whether the United
Kingdom would take the initiative in sumoning such a conference, he replied
that he very much doubted that the United Kingdom could do so. He felt that
the United States, being "in charge" in Japan, would necessarily have to
take the initiative. He volunteered (as his personal opinion) the informe-
tion that Hr. Den ing would head the Wited Kingdem Delegation to the Peace
Conference. He also said that he had invited Mr. Dening to visit Japan
during Ootober 1948 for several weeks, in order that he might obtain first-
hand information of the situation here.
On the subject of the economy of Japan, Sir Alvary said that the
Foreign Office is in full agreement with the United States position that a
viable oconomy is necessary for Japan. It is his opinion that the United
States can expect full support from the United Kingdom in its objectives in
SECRET
this regand.

Dear George:
I am becoming daily more and more worried about
xR
the whole Japanese situation, and am wondering whether ne diree-
tive was sent out to sCAp based on the admirable recommendations
you made after you returned.
711.94
A man who was just he re from Japan the other day
said that what we seemed to be doing out there was to lay down
the red carpet to welcome the Soviet. The purging does not sem
to have stopped, and I understand that now there is a fairly
strong faction, formerly American in sympathy, smong the Japanese,
which is now planning to start an anti-American group. More and
more people are turning toward the Soviet because they feel that
the Americans in Tokyo certainly do not represent what we preach
as to the nature of democracy. I do not care particularly what
the Japanese say and think, except that I kmow there are many.
and probably an extremely large proportion of very fine, forward-
looking people in that country. What I do feel from the bottom
of my heart is that if, through our stupidity, we pormit Russia
to take over in Japan, which would mean, of course, the loss of
the Philippines and all of Asia to communism, we might just as
well begin building a wall around this country and try to live
our own lives as best we may.
Of course, I realize fully that it is not for me
to butt in on State Department matters, but I nevertheless be-
lieve that every decent American ought to do his little bit toward
preventing what seems at the moment the almost unpreventable ad-
vance of the Soviet everywhere. Unless we are exceedingly care-
ful on the Oclonial question, we are going to lose Italy. And
Italy is just about the best friend we have in Western Europe,
Just as Japan is the only friend we have left in Asia.
I wish m could lunch together some day because I
should like to talk with you about all these matters. But I know
how terribly busy you are and, therefore, shall understand if you
8
say there is no possibility of getting together.
94.00
Very sincerely,
Biee
Mr. George Kennan,

Subject: Left Wing Political Realignments.
