I have the honor to refer to this Mission's
despatch No. 774 of December 9, 1948 concerning political
repercussions resulting from revision of the National
Public Service Law, and to bring to the Department's
attention the extent to which important realignments
appear to be forming among left wing political groups.
Disintegration of Social Democratic Party
1
The failure of the Social Democratic Party to
support revision of the Public Service Law after an
earlier pledge to do so has touched off a heated contro-
versy which threatens to split the party still further,
or to bring about what Yomiuri Shimbun has described
as the party's "mid-air disintegration". From the time
of its organization in November l945, the Social Democratic
Party has been characterized by internal dissension among
its complex components. The party has not enjoyed strong
leadership and has had to depend upon various compromise
agreements among its conflicting factions. Mr. KATAYAMA
Tetsu, head of the party and former Prime Minister, is
himself the epitome of such compromise. Although opposed
to communist extremes, ir. Katayama would, if he had his
choice, pursue a policy of thorough-going socialization,
but he has had to make continual political compromises
with more conservative elements both within and outside
his own party.
Until
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 300 === (confidence 0.99)
Tokyo's Despatch No. 813,
December 29, 1948.
CONFIDENTIAL
-2-
Until recently, the right wing of the Social Democratic
Party, centering around the Toitsu Kondan Kai (Unity
Conference Group), held the balance of power in party
affairs. The purge of Mr. HIRANo Rikizo and the involve-
ment of Mr. NISHIo Suehiro and Mr. NAGAE Kazuo in political
scandals has seriously undermined the power and prestige
of the right wing. On the other hand, the left wing's
influence within the party has not correspondingly
increased. In July 1948 Mr. KURODA Hisao was read out
of the party because of his strong opposition to compromise
policies, and many members of his farmer-labor group
subsequently seceded in protest. Another left wing leader,
Ir. ARAHATA Kanson, has also withdrawn and is planning to
organize a "reformed" socialist party of his own.
While these right and left wing defections have
taken place, other malcontent elements remaining in the
party have begun agitating for either a drastic reorgani-
zation or the disbandment of the party. Some dissatisfied
right wing members believe that a change of leadership,
eliminating Mr. Katayama, Mr. MATSUOKA Komakichi, and
kr. ASANUMA Inajiro, would give the party new life since
these leaders have become too closely identified with
vacillating shifts and compromises.
Dissatisfied left wing elements still remaining
within the party are also demanding its reorganization
or disbandment. A left wing group affiliated with the
Japan Farmers Union is contemplating the organization
of an anti-communist socialist party based upon the
support of the proposed new National Congress of Industrial
Union (NCIU). Heretofore, the Social Democratic Party's
labor support has come almost entirely from the General
Federation of Trade Unions, while the NCIU, through the
influence of communist fractions, has supported the
Japan Communist Party. During the past year anti-communist
leaders in the NCIU have organized Democratization Leagues
(Minshu-ka Domei) and have challenged the predominant
position of the comnunists. The Democratization League
groups are now attempting to bring about the organization
of a "reformed", non-communist NCIU.
Another left wing group in the party, which also
demands disbandment, has proposed the organization of a
pro-communist socialist party which might become affiliated
with the new Labor-Farmer rarty (described below) of
Mr. Kuroda Hisao and form a popular front with the communists.
This group has a number of former communists affiliated
with it such as Mr. KATSUi.ATA Seiichi.
Still another left wing Social Democrat, Mir. YAliAKAWA
Hitoshi, who before the war was one of the leaders in
the Japan Communist rarty, has also issued a call for
disbandment.
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 301 === (confidence 0.99)
Tokyo's Despatch No. 813,
December 29, 1948.
CONFIDENTIAL
-3-
disbandment. In the 1920's Mr. Yamakawa wes the center
of a dispute which almost split the communist party
(the famous Yamakawa-Fukumoto controversy which the
Comintern was finally compelled to settle with its
1927 "Thesis"). Later Yamakawa drifted away from the
party and became identified with the popular front
movement in the late 1930's, and joined the Social
Democretic Party at the end of the war. Mr. Yamakawa
has never felt at home with the socialists and has
periodically expressed a desire for a popular front
with the communists.
In the December 13 issue of Yomiuri Shimbun
Mr. Yamakawa explained his views on the need to disband
the present Social Democratic Party which he declared
is "now entirely isolated from the class which represents
socialistic tendencies". The party therefore must be
reconstructed upon the basis of "the class which supports
socialism". Mr. Yamakawa views the decision of the
party to oppose revision of the Public Service Law as
a belated and insincere effort to meet the demands of
labor. In Mr. Yamakawa's opinion, the present party
should dissolve because it has failed to keep in contact
with the working masses "through revolutionary action".
It is believed that if ir. Yamakawa is successful in
reforming the present party or organizing a new one,
his efforts will be premised on the possibility of
achieving a popular front with the communists.
The New Labor-Farmer Party
The most significant left wing activity thus
far undertaken has been the establishment on December 3,
1948 of the new Labor-Farmer Party (Rodosha Nomin To,
commonly abbreviated as Rono To), headed by Mr. Kuroda
Hisao who was expelled from the Social Democratic Party
in July 1948.
The Rono To is a manifestation of left wing discontent
with the relatively conservative policies pursued by the
Social Democratic Party under the leadership of Chairman
5.1
Katayama Tetsu and Secretary General Asanuma Inajiro.
The new party poses as an independent group, standing
between the socialists and the communists. A declaration
of principles issued at the time of the party's inauguration
charges that the Social Jemocretic Party "has degenerated
into a bourgeois party by abandonment of its class
struggle." At the same time, the declaration accuses the
Japan Conmunist Party of becoming "dogmatic" and failing
to guarantee the interests of the working masses. In
effect, the new party argues that the socialists are too
bourgeois to benefit the masses while the conmunists are
too radical to be practical. The position taken by the
Rono To,
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 302 === (confidence 0.99)
. Tokyo's Despatch No. 813,
December 29, 1948.
CONFIDENTIAL
-4-
Rono To, however, is more opposed to the Social Democratic
Party than to the Japan Communist rarty.
Communist Interest in Labor-Farmer Party
It is of significance, therefore, that the communists
have evinced keen interest in the new-born Rono To.
Mr. NOSAKA Sanzo of the Japan Communist Party appeared
as a speaker at one of the new party's preparatory rallies.
The communist party is not likely to permit one of its
top leaders to appear at the rally of another party unless
this is expected to prove advantageous to the communists.
Conversely, it is not likely that Mr. Kuroda would launch
his new party with a communist party speaker on the platform
if he did not believe that evidence of such friendly
relations with the communists will prove advantageous.
Questioned by a reporter of Shin Tokyo (issue of December 6)
as to how a line of demarcation could be drawn between the
Rono To and the conmunist party, Mr. Kuroda reportedly
replied: "The comunist party is also struggling for the
sake of democratic revolution. However, it often leans to
extreme leftist behaviorism in neglect of power relation-
ships in class strife. It is not as if we had drawn a
definite line against it, but we do believe that with the
communist party alone the democratic revolution would be
difficult to achieve." In the same issue of Shin Tokyo
Mr. Nosaka was also interviewed on the subject of the
Rono To. While suggesting that the new party contains
some anti-communist elements, r. Nosaka added: "Of course,
there are some fine individuals in this party, especially
among the rank and file. I would like to continue our
struggles hereafter in close cooperation with these
persons. Also, there are some in this party who support
scientific, revolutionary Socialism and Marxism. I think
such persons should voluntarily join the communist party,
just as the socialists in Aomori did."
It is also significant that the communist party
daily, Akahata, has accorded the new Rono To considerable
uncritical publicity. Communist publications seldon
devote space to straight news reporting; their articles
usually propagandize. It may be assumed, therefore,
that the Japan Communist Party views with approval the
appearance of a seemingly rival party at the extreme left
of the political stage. Mr. Kuroda himself is a former
member of the Japen Communist rarty. Among those assist-
ing him in the organization of the new party are a number
of well known communist sympathizers, believed to be
secret communist party members, such as Mr. YOSHIDA
Sukeharu of the National Federation of Metal Mine Workers,
a nuuber of representatives of the communist-dominated
National Congress of Industrial Unions, and of the
communist front Jemocracy rrotection League. The peculiar
atmosphere
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 303 === (confidence 0.99)
Tokyo's Despatch No. 813,
December 29, 1948.
CONFIDENTIAL
-5-
atmosphere which has attended the organization of the
Rono To strongly suggests that this new left wing political
party is itself a skilfully conceived communist front
group.
Commenting on the two parties, Tokyo Shimbun in
its issue of December 7 noted that "the platform and
slogans of the two parties are so nearly alike that we
may fairly call them the same". This paper further noted
that "there is a considerable group of voters disappointed
with the socialists but hesitant to support the communists;
if the party is guided wisely, the Labor-Farmer Party
which claims 20,000 party members, can win this group over."
Renewed Interest in a Popular Front
All evidence indicates that the communists have
recently placed more emphasis than ever before on the use
of fronts. Recent notable examples are the organization
of the Farmer-Lapor kelief Association in the summer of
1948, and the appearance of the Democracy rrotection League
in August, 1948. The latter organization has served pri-
marily as a social and cultural front in carrying out
communist opposition to revision of the National rublic
Service Law. A number of leftists associated with these
two major front organizations are also active in the newly-
created Rono To.
In giving indirect support to the Rono To, it appears
that the Japan Comaunist Party has made a significant change
in its political strategy. Heretofore, front groups have
been used by the Japanese communists primarily as agencies
to implement the party's policies and, where possible, to
secure political support for the party itself. For example,
the Democracy Protection Lea ue assists the party's agita-
tion against revision of the Public Service Law by giving
the appearance that the comunist party is only one of many
groups opposed to revision. at the same time, by high-
lighting the comamunist party's position on the issue, the
Democracy Protection League endeavors to create greater
non-communist interest in and support of the prograin of the
comnunist party.
If the Rono To is a communist front, however, the
communist party is in the position of encouraging the growth
of a rival political party. Outwardly, this might apear to
be dangerous strategy, but the encourugement of seemingly
rival political parties has similarly been pursued by
communists in other countries. The Japan Communist Party,
like the comunist party in the United States, is under no
illusion about its inability to win a strong enough position
in elections to determine the oliticul future of the country.
In these circunstunces the communist party in the United
States gave its unyualified support to r. Henry WALLACE's
Progressive Party in the last presidential election, because
the conunists were p arently convinced that they could
work efreet vely with and through Mr. Wallace's group.
It appears that the Japan Communist Party hus reached
a si ilar conclusion with respect to Mr. Kuroda's Rono To.
While the Japan Communist Party will push its own political
campi n
CONFIDENTIAL

=== Page 304 === (confidence 0.99)
Tokyo's Despatch No. 813,
December 29, 1948.
CONFIDENTIAL
-6-
campaign quite independently, its leaders unquestionably
realize that there is still a large liberal and left wing
element which is not yet prepared to join the communists
or to support communist candidates. Normally such liberals
and leftists affiliate with or support the Social Democratic
Party. Soon after the beginning of the Cccupation, before
political alignments were as clearly defined as today,
the Japanese communists nade repeated attempts to interest
the Social Jemocratic Party in a popular front merger. The
socialists, however, consistently rejected this effort to
infiltrate their ranks, although the party's left wing
was always partial tovard tie popular front idea. The
Japanese communists rinelly decided that it was futile to
tempt the Social Democratic Party with such bait. Popular
front proposals were dropped about the middle of 1946 and
have not since been revived.
Now, however, the position of the Social Democratic
Party has changed considerably. It has suffered in prestige
and vote appeal. It has been weakened by conflicts among
its varied elements, some of which have broken away from
the party. Other strong leaders have been lost as a
result of the purge or implication in political scandals.
Such a party no longer offers an attraction to the communists
as a popular front merger, although the comaunists are
again showing interest in such a strategy.
The advent of the nono To, as a new left wing
party already having twelve members in the House of Repre-
sentatives and apparently cohesive and free of internal
conflicts, offers the Japanese communists an advantageous
opportunity for coordinated action. The Rono To is
radical enough for the communists to feel safe in cooper-
ating with it; yet it is not so radical that it will
alarm liberals and leftists who have been afraid to
support the comnunist party. The communists apparently
believe that the radical elements in the labor and farmer
unions can be counted upon to support cosmunist party
candidates through the activities of conmunist cell
members and fractions in these bodies. (This unquestion-
ably explains the decision to have r. DOBa3HI Kazuyoshi,
head of the All-Japan Communication Norkers Union,
formally join the conmunist party and run for the Diet
as a communist candidate.) A further utility seen by
the coamunists in propagating good relations with the
Rono To lies in meeting the threat of the strong anti-
communist bloc in the National Congress of Industrial
Unions (which has been organized around the various
Democratization League). Democratization League followers
would ordinarily be expected to support the Social Demo-
cratic Party, and the party's leftist have already
begun working closely with league groups. The communists
may have in mind attempting to neutralize the Democratiza-
tion League's anti-communist activity in the labor move-
ment by diverting its political strength to the Rono To.
The
JONFIDENTIAL

Tokyo's Despatch No.' 813,
December 29, 1948,
CONFIDENTIAL
-7-
The Rono To is as yet an exceedingly small party,
and lacks a leader of national reputation. There are
some indications, however, that Mr. Kuroda's position
as head of the party is a temporary one notwithstanding
his role in establishing the party. Considerable
significance, therefore, is attached to persistent reports
that the Rono To is conducting quiet negotiations with
Mr. OYAMA Ikuo in an effort to induce him to join the
party and take over its leadership. Since his return to
Japan in 1947 after a long exile in the United States,
Mr. Oyama has abstained from direct participation in
politics or direct affiliation with any political party.
This has surprised most leftist Japanese who expected
that this veteran socialist and former leader of the pre-
war Rono To would take an active part in politics. Mr. Oyama,
however, has preferred to pursue a cautious course and
has avoided all political commitments. On the other hand,
he has taken great pains, through lecture tours and prolific
writing for the press, to keep his name before the Japanese
public. It is quite possible that kr. Oyama is playing
a waiting game, hoping that out of the present realignment
of left wing political forces he may be called upon to
head a popular front movement.
Communist-Socialist Merger"
Wile the Rono To appears to enjoy apparent communist
party sponsorship, other left wing elements from the Social
Democratic Party are entering into open alliance with the
Japanese communists. In Aomori Prefecture a number of
Social Democrats, led by Mr. OS.A Kyumei, have broken
away from their party and openly joined the communists.
A similar movement has already begun in Niigata Prefecture,
Nagano Prefecture, and several other areas. The communist
party is actively supporting the communist-socialist merger
drive in the prefectures. The communists, however, make
it clear that this "merger" is a one-sided transaction.
In its is ue of December 10, Akahata declared that "the
merger can succeed only when communist party decisions
and policies are faithfully observed."
These developments in the left wing political area
suggest that an important realignment of leftist forces
is now taking place. From the time of its organization
at the end of the war, the Social Democratic Party was
a political anomaly, which attempted to incorporate in
one body a wide range of political sentiment. It tried
to cover the fielu fron the boundary of conservativisi.
(as represented by the Democratic-Liberal und Democratic
parties) to the boundery of ultra-radicalism (as repre-
sented by the Japan Communist Party). Such wide coverage
necessitated
CONFIDE.TIAL

=== Page 306 === (confidence 0.99)
Tokyo's Despatch No. 813,
December 29, 1948.
CONFIDENTIAL
-8-
necessitated a strange merger of conservative and radical
opinion which has proved to be an unworkable political
alliance.
Conclusions
The trends described in this despatch suggest that
a more clearly defined realignment of political forces
is now taking place. Unfortunately, however, this
realignment is at the expense of the middle groupings
from which it woili.ost desirable that a sound labor
party should emerge. While the political center is
tending to disintegrate, the conservative forces repre-
sented by the Democratic-Liberal and Democratic Parties
are likely to merge into a single, conservative party.
If such a situation develops, it appears possible that
the only effective opposition to the conservative right
will be an extreme left wing front under communist leader-
ship. In our view a far more desirable and practicable
political pattern to encourage democratic development in
Japan would be a conservative group facing a labor type
of political party rather than a conservative group faced
by an extree leftist front. It is also believed that a
formidable leftist opposition under communist leadership
will tend to make the conservative right still more con-
servative if not reactionary.
However desirable may be a final patterning of
Japanese parties into alternating conservative and labor
majorities, with the communists confined to a small minority,
the developments outlined above indicate that the communists
are bending every effort to take advantage of the prevailing
disorganization in the parties in the area between right
and left and are striving to attract to the communist sphere
of control and influence a sufficiently la rge political
following to assure the communists much more than a small
minority position.
Respectfully yours,
. J. Sebald

SUMMARY
The proletarian movement in Japan originated in the industrialization of
the 1870's but did not become of any great importance until after World War I.
Between 1918 and the passage of the universal manhood suffrage law in 1925,
organized proletarian efforts were devoted largely to the establishment of trade
unions. The granting of universal manhood suffrage, however, stimulated the
organization of proletarian political parties that were supported by and worked
closely with the trade-union federations.
From its inception in the 1870's to the end of World War II, the Japanese
labor movement operated within a framework of severe government repression of
both its political and economic activities. Major legislation as well as police
regulations limited the content of the programs of unione and parties and subjected
their activities to constant police surveillance and interference, their meetings to
abrupt terminations, their organizations to frequent dissolutions and their leadership
to intermittent arrest.
In establishing policy, therefore, the political leadership of the proletarian
movement not only had to reconcile conflicting elements within its own ranks and to
compromise on certain issues in order to make possible the broadening of its support
but also had to seek at all times to stay within the limits of the logally allowablo.
Since government interpretation of these limits tended to be variable and unpredictable,
proletarian party programs, in turn, tended to be vague at best and inconsistent at
worst.
The ideological controversy common to labor moveonts was, if anything,
sharpened by government suppression, and only from 1936 to 1939 was unity attained
on the left. From the end of World War I to the beginning of the period of Japanese
expansion on the Asiatic continent in 1931, the major ideological split was that
between the Social Democrats and their supporters on the one hand and the Communists
RESTRICTED

=== Page 318 === (confidence 0.98)
- 11 -
RESTRICTED
and their sympathizers on the other. During this period there were frequent moves
for the amalgamation of the various proletarian parties. Most of these moves
failed partially or completely. The primary reason for their failure seems to
have been the controversy over admission of left-wing elements to the coalition,
but personal rivalries undoubtedly were a contributing factor.
By l932, however, the effectiveness of government suppression of the
Commmmist movement and the incarceration or flight of most of its leaders had
considerably reduced the importance of the controversy over the Communist issue.
Meanwhile, a new issue had arisen to take its place -- the controversy between
those elements in the proletarian movement that, in a period of heightening
patriotic fervor, veered in the direction of national socialiem and those that
attempted to remain loyal to the principles of social democracy even while
retreating under pressure from their more radical position of the past. Although
this controversy resulted initially in the complete splitting-off of the most
convinced national socialists and the amalgamation of the remaining groups into
the Shakai Taishuto, the dominant proletarian party of the 1930's, it ended in
1940 in complete disunity and the disappearance, under government pressure, of
organized labor as an independent force.
During the war active Japenese radicaliem was confined to small groupe of
exiles and prisoners of war in China. In Japan proper, labor disturbances and
slackening morale were occasionally attributed to Communist or other leftist
activities, but no evidence has emerged of any significant wartime underground.
In China there were two centers of Japanese radicaliem -- one in the Kuomintang
area and one in the aree under Commumiat control. In Nationaliet China, Japanese
radical activities hardly constituted a movement, since they were confined to a
very large extent to the assistance rendered to Allied pyschological warfare by two
RESTRICTED

=== Page 319 === (confidence 0.98)
- x111 -
RESTRICTED
extremely small groups of Japanese prisoners, each led by a Japanese exile. In the
Communist area, on the other hand, use of Japanese prisoners in peychological
warfare led to the organization of a movement that, although amall and limited in
its activities, was important because of the training it gave its members in
organizational and indoctrination techniques and the groundwork it established for
present-day Commumist united front efforts.
The organization of the Nippon Shakaito (Socialist Party) in November 1945
not only represented the revival of organized social democracy in Japan but also
demonstrated the willingness of right- and left-wing social democrats and former
national socialists to bury their past differences, to some extent at least, in
order to achieve unity of action in the present and future. The revival of the
Nippon Kyōsantō (Communist Party), on the other hand, and the strength that 1t
derived from its new freedom intensified conflict among the factions of the
Shakaitō by raising the united front issue to a position of greater prominence than
it had ever occupied in prewar Japan. At the seme time, the new strength of the
Socialists raised the parallel and equally controversial issue of cooperation with
the conservative parties.
Proposals for a Commmist-Socialist united front were first made by the
Communiste in the early daye of the occupation, when both parties were still in
the process of organization. Despite considerable press support for the united
front idea, however, the pressure exerted in its favor by left-wing Socialiets, the
Shakaito decided in January 1946 to postpone decision until after the lower house
election scheduled for April 1946.
In the April election the Socialists polled about 9 million votes and elected
93 members, while the Communists polled about 2 million votes and seated 5 candidates.
Since the two conservative parties, the Liberals and the Progressives, hed seated 141
RESTRICTED

=== Page 320 === (confidence 0.98)
- 1v -
RESTRICTED
and 93 candidates respectively, it was apparent that a coalition would be essential
for the formation of a cabinet with some prospect for stability. Similarity of the
background and attitudes of the Liberals and Progressives may perhaps have made
inevitable their ultimate cooperation in the formation of a government. Rivalries
and ambitions, to some extent inherited from the prewar period, were sufficiently
strong, however, to lead each of the two conservative parties to consider the
possibility of joint action with a third party. In thie situation, the bargaining
power of the Socialists was fairly strong but their ability to use it was diminished
by the issues of principle upon which the party was split, issues in which the
question of collaboration with the Commmists played an important part. After forty
days of interparty negotiations, in which strong Commmist pressure was exerted
against Socialist participation in a Liberal-Progressive coalition, the two
conservative parties joined in support of the Yoshida cabinet and the attention of
the Left was focused once again on the united front problem.
In united front discussions it soon became apparent that the Shakaito envisaged
a united front in which party representatives in the Diet would dominate, whereas the
Commnnists, aware of their Diet weakmess, sought the formation of a popular front in
which trade unions and other mass organizations with relatively strong Commmiet
influonce would participate on an equal basis with the parties. After prolonged
discussions, marked once again by internal Socialist controversy and by the exercise
of Commnist pressure through organizations under their influence as well as
through the party itself, the Shakaitō in July 1946 finally decided to exclude the
Commnists from the united front organization to be set up under Socialist auspices.
By the fall of 1946, discontent with the Yoshida cabinet had lod Yoshida himself
to consider strengthening the coalition by inducing the Socialists to enter it.
The onsuing negotiations in December 1946-January 1947 culminated in reorganization
of the existing coalition and were in many respects similar to the negotiations of
the preceding May before the original formation of the Yoshida cabinet.
RESTRICTED

=== Page 321 === (confidence 0.98)
-7 -
RESTRICTED
In both periods, the Shakaito was rent internally over the issue of cooperation
with the conservative parties. Comnmists and left-ving Socialists alike utilized
widespread labor discontent to put pressure on right-wing Socialists and on the
government for the formation of a Socialist-centered cabinet, which was widely
demanded by the press. The similarities between the Liberals end Progressives
were sufficiently strong to outweigh their differences and lead them to ultimate
cooperation.
The differences between the two periods, although less striking, were of
great potential importance. In the first place, the issue of a umited front
between the Socialists and Commmiste, which played so important a role in the
earlier crisis, did not arise in the latter period, when the Comamists were
politically isolated, exerting their influence through certain trade unions rather
than through the party and its Diet representatives. Secondly, internal divisions
within the two conservative parties had become considerably stronger and an important
Progressive faction had moved somewhat closer in its program to the Socialists.

PART ONE: THE JAPANESE PROLETARIAN MOVEENT IN THE
PRE-SURRENDER PERIOD
I. THE PROLETARIAN MOVEENT, 1918-1940
A. Major Characteristics
1. Introduction. The proletarian movemsent in Japan originated in the
industrialization of the 1870's but did not become of any great importance
until after World War I. Between 1918 and the passage of the universal manhood
suffrage law in l925 organized proletarian efforts were devoted largely to the
establishment of trade unions. The granting of universal manhood suffrage,
however, stimulated the organization of proletarian political parties that
2. Goverment Suppression. From its inception in the 1870's to the end
of World War II, the Japanese labor movement operated within a framework of
severe goverment repression of both its political and economic activities.
Major legislation as well as police regulations limited the content of union
and party programs and subjected their activities to constant police surveillance
and interference, their meetings to ebrupt termination, their organizations to
The existence of government suppression not only weakened the labor
movement directly but also had other important consequences on its development.
The weakmess of labor's legal position made it necessary for the movements that
represented its interests to devote considerable effort, in a period fairly late
in their development, to attempts to gain legal recognition for trade unions,
1. This paper is concerned with the political aspects of the proletarian movement
and will discuss the trade umions in that context only. It should be noted
that the political attitudes and activities of the Japanese trade unions have
at all times been similar to those of European rather than American labor
movements.

collective bargaining, and the right to strike. Hampered in this struggle by
repressive government policies, the trade umions were further weakened both in
terms of organization and of membership by being forced to fight simultaneously
for basic rights and the day-to-day interests of their members. This weakmese,
in turn, was reflected in the political parties that the trade unions supported.
Even more important, perhaps, for the development of the political movement
was the fact that at no time was labor free to express its program as fully,
vehemently or radically as it might desire. In establishing policy, therefore,
the political leadership of the prolotarian movement not only had to reconcile
conflicting elements within its own ranks and to compromise on certain issues in
order to make possible the broadening of its support, but also had to seek at all
times to stay within the limits of the legally allowable. Since government
interpretation of these limits tended to be variable and unpredictable,
proletarian party programs, in turn, tended to be vague at best and inconsistent
at woret.
3. Ideological Controversy. The ideological controversy common to labor
movements was thus, if anything, sharpened by government suppression. A union
of right-and-left-wing groups, for example, can always be expected to cause a loss
of ideological purity to both factions involved, and the attempt to prevent this
loss may ultimately produce controversy more bitter than that which the original
amalgamation was designed to ameliorate. In Japan, the natural hesitancy,
particularly on the part of the right wing, to enter into such potentially
disruptive alliances was heightened by fear, again generally on the part of right-
wing groups, that alliances would cause the government to extend to the movement
as a whole the very severe repressive measures that it had utilized against left-
wing groups. In consequence, emalgamation of proletarian groupa were frequently
regarded as a source of voakness rather than of strength; and, in this atmosphere,
ideological differences, reinforced by personal rivalries tended to flourish out

From the end of World War I to the beginning of the period of Japanese

that between the Social Democrats and their supporters on the one hand and the
Commmists and their sympathizers on the other. During this period there were

loyal to the principles of social democracy even while retreating under pressure
from their more radical position of the past. Although this controversy resulted
initially in the complete splitting-off of the most convinced national socialists
and the emalgamation of the remaining groups into the Shakai Taishuto, the
dominant proletarian party of the l930's, it ended in complote disumity and the
disappearence under government pressure of organized labor as an independent force.

It was not long before socialist organizations, trade unions, and strikos appeared.
Despite official disfavor, frequently manifesting itself in arrests, interruption
of meetings, suspension of publications, and dissolution of organizations, a number

Although economic conditions in Japan might be expected to lead directly to

Under both rightist and leftist leadership, moreover, the Nippon Kyōsantō had

The new line was laid down in all its essential points in the roport to the
Congress by the Bulgarian Commmmist, Georgi Dimitroff. Its principal features were a
new interpretation of the nature and dangers of fascism and, in consequence, a new
attitude toward both social democrats and political democracy. In Dimitroff's report,
fascism was defined as the "terrorist dictatorship of the most reactionary, most
chauvinistic and most imperialist elements of finence capital," the spearheed of
international counterrevolution, the chief incendiary of imperialist war, and the
initiator of a crusade against the workers' fatherland, the Soviet Union. Its rise
to power, Dimitroff declared, had been accomplished because the working class had
been politically and organizationally split. Its defeat required not only a umited
front of all working class organizations, whether socialist, communist, or religious,
but also the establishment of an anti-fascist peoplee' front based on an alliance
between the proletariat on the one hand and the peasantry and the middle classes
on the other. He asserted that the only condition that should be established for
the achievement of this unity was that it "be directed against fasciem, against the
offensive of capital, against the threat of war, against the class enemy." Furthermore,

II. THE LXIT IN EXIIE
A. Introduction
Active Japanese radicalism during the war was confined to mmall groups of eriles
and prisoners of war in China. In Japan proper, labor disturbances and slackening
morale were occasionally attributed to Commmist or other leftist activities, but
no evidence has emerged of any significant underground organization during the war.
Indeed, Japanese Commnists -- with practically all of their leaders in prison --
seem to have consciously adopted a program of quietiam in an attempt to conserve
their strength and avoid unnecessary sacrifices. On the whole, Commmist
activities during the war period seem to have been confined to cautious attempts
by individuals to influence their fellows.
In China, there were two centers of Japanose radicaliem -- one in the
Kuomintang area and one in the area under Communist control. In nationalist China,
Japanese radical activities hardly constituted a movement, since they were confined
to a very large extent to the assistance rendered to Allied psyohological warfare by
two ertremely small groups of Japanese prisoners led respectively by KAJI Wataru and
AOYAMA Kazuo, both exiled radicals. In the Commumist area, on the other hand, use
of Japanese prisoners in psychological warfare led to the organization of a
movement that, although amall and limited in its activities, was important because
of the training it gave its members in organizational and indostrination techmiques
and the groundwork it established for post-war Commmiet united-front efforts.
B. The Japanese in Commmist China
1. Early Policies of the Chinese Commmists. During the civil war period
(1927-l937) the Chinese Commnists had made extensive use of peychological warfare
techniques, particularly those directed at converting the onemy as well as
demoralizing him. It was but natural, therefore, that they should think in terms of
adapting those techniques to the war against the Japanese. Early efforts were based
almost entirely upon civil war models; Chinese soldiers shouted slogans in Japanese
RESTRICTED

=== Page 377 === (confidence 0.98)
- 52 -
RESTRICTED
calling upon the enemy to surrender and promising good treatment. This techmique
proved ineffectual, however, and late in l937 more serious attention was given to
the problem by the Political Affairs Department of the Eighth Route Army. It was
announced that the general population in Communist areas and all troops, were to be
instructed in so-called anti-enemy work; that special anti-eneuy units were to be
formed; and that war prisoners were not to be killed but to be given preferential
treatmont.1
The political basis for this type of work was laid in an order issued by Chu Teh
that declared: "Japanese soldiers are the sons and brothers of the toiling masses.
Deceived and coerced by the Japanese warlords and financial oligarchs, they have been
forced to fight against us." It was therefore necessary to expose Japanese
propaganda, to heighten the war-weariness and anti-war sentiments of the Japanese
soldiers, and to offer them a way out by urging them to fight against their government's
war of aggression. Practically, this was to be achieved by forbidding injury or
insult to Japanese prisoners, giving special care to the wounded, releasing those
who wished to return to their units and doing everything possible to achieve their
safe return, erecting tombstores for Japanese soldiers killed in battle, and providing
suitable work and educational facilities for those prisoners who wished to remain
with the Eighth Route Army.2
Successes achieved, however, were extremely limitod. It was discovered from
discuseion with the few Japanese who were taken prisoner and decided to remain with
the Commumists that the slogans the latter had been employing in their leaflets were
far too radical and abstract to obtain sympathy or even comprehension from the average
Japanese soldier.3 Recognition of these and other weaknesses led to an attempt to

According to the Appeal, the most important task of the Japanese people was to
bring the war to an end by organizing a people's front, crushing the militarists,
and setting up a people's govermment. To achieve thie objective, the politically
conscious were: to enlighten the people with regard to the true nature of the war;
to encourage them to reject their war-born burden of sacrifice; to urge them to unite
and fight to protect their own livelihood and liberty; and by these means to seek to
render Japan's wartime structure unstable. The first step in the struggle was the
fight for the immediate demands of the people. These demands, like those of the
Japanese soldiers, ranged from the conceivably possible, such as an increase in
wages and on improvement in air raid shelters, to such demands as the recall of
husbands, brothers, and sons from the front, the achievement of which would
require the overthrow of the government and the end of the war.
Although the Appeal was thus more of a lesson in how discontent might be
exploited for political ends than a considered statement of policy, its political
aspects at least gave some indication of the aims that were both acceptable to Nosaka
and his follovers and regarded by them as having some appeal for the Japanese people.
The process by which the people's government was to be established was described in
general terms. Complete freedom of speech, press, assembly, and organization was
to be granted; all political prisoners were to be released; suffrage was to be granted
to all men and women over twenty; free elections were to be held; and the Diet so
elected was to be givon full rights by a revised constitution. On the basis of this
Diet and constitution, a people's government was to be set up.

PART TWO:
THE REVIVAL OF LEFT-WING ORGANIZATIONS IN THE PERIOD AFTER THE SURRENDER
INTRODUCTION
The aituation in which the proletarian movement was revived in Japan was
similar in some respects to that which saw its inauguretion us a political force.
The occunation produced a new political situation -- much more revolutionary in its
impect, of course, than the crant of universal manhood suffrage -- in which it was
apparent that a united party representing the interests of Japan's proletariat and
peas ntry might hope to exert considerable influence over Japan's future. The
removal of the danger of government suppression and the guarantee of civil
liberties implicit in the presence of an occupying force dedicated to the
establishment of democracy in Japan removed one factor that had militated against
the achievement of proletarian unity in the past. Prewar experience of the
disadvantages of disunity also pointed to the desirability of compromise in order
to secure united action on major issues. It was questionable, on the other hand,
to what extent such united action could be achieved in practice, since some if not
all of the factors that had prevented unity in the pest continued to be of
considerable importance.
From 1926 to 1931 the proletarian movement had developed along two main lines,
social democratic and commmist, with many divergencies within each of the two main
groups. Beginning with the 193o's, however, national socialism, closely allied with
expansionism, became increasingly important as a source of conflict within the
proletarien movement. The postwar movement has inherited the conflict between social
democracy and communism, a conflict that has been intensified by international
developments. For the immediate future, however, the issue of nationalist,
expansionist socialism has been reduced to insignificance, and the dispute of the
past is important today only so far as it jeopardizes the leadership position of th
those returning to the proleterian movement who, whether from reasons of principle
RESTRICTED

RESTRICTED
or expediency, actively collaboreted with the wartime government.
The organization of the Nippon Shakaitō (Socinlist Party of Japan) in November
1945 not only represented the revivel of orcanized social democracy in Japen but
also demonstrated the willin/ness of right- and left-wing social democrats end former
national socialists to bury their past differences, to some extent at least, in
order to achieve unity of action in the present and future. The revival of the
Nippon Kyōsanto (Communist Party of Japan), on the other hand and the strength

B. Program and Policy
1
1. General Objectives and Strategy. The long-term objectives of the Shakaito
are the achievement of a democratic socialiem in which the basic means of production
and distribution will be socialized and small-scale enterprise will be organized as
far as possible on a cooperative basis. These objectives are to be realized through
the attainment of a parliamentary majority and the utilization of parliamentary
machinery to effect economic reform. Like the Communists, the Socialists regard
trade unions and other non-party organizations as important channels for the spread
of their influence and as outlets for the expression of their economic and political
aims. They differ, however, both from the Commmists and among themselves, with
regard to the weight that they place upon parliementary as opposed to extra-
parliamentary tactics. Among right-wing Socialiste there is a tendency to rely.
heavily on party politics and to regard the trade unions, for political purposes,
as sources of numerical strength rather than leadership. The leftists, on the other
hand, tend to look with greater favor upon extra-parliamentary political leaderehip
by the trade unions and more readily accept the techmique of mass pressure as a
mothod of influencing government policy.
2. Political
a. The Emperor question. The Shakaitō early committed 1tself to the
principle that democratic socialism could be attained under an Emperor who was shorn
of all actual political power.2 Despite some initial uncertainty with regard to
the Emperor question and despite the fact that the Central Executive Committee's
willingness to accept retention of the Emperor was one element in the much-publicized

Individual Socialists -- TAKANO Iwasaburo and MATSUMOTO Jiichiro, for example --
have expressed themselves forcibly as favoring a republican form of government for
Japan, but this question, unlike others, has not been the occasion for a split
between the left and right wings. In point of fact one of the strongest Socialist
statements in favor of retaining the Emperor was made by KATo Kanju himself, who
declared:
"From the standpoint of modern legal theory, democracy may be
irreconcilable with the Japanese national structure. From the earliest
period down to recent times, however, the Emperor has always been
regarded as head of the national family, and the relation between the
Emperor and the people has never been that of the conqueror and the
conquered.
"From this point of view, Japanese monarchy and democracy are
perfectly compatible with each other. It should rather be said that
democracy with the Emperor as head of the national family is the true
tradition of Japan. It has always been the class or classes intervening
between the Emperor and the people that prevented the development of
national government in the direction of democracy. Owing to the
influence of the intervening classes, no political reform in the past
has been thorough. A radical reconstruction of national government is,
therefore abeolutely necessary, but the Emperor will remain as a symbol
of national reverence."2
b. Constitutional reform. In prewar Japan the proletarian parties had been
limited by fear of government suppression to demanas for basic political reform
couched in the most general of terme. They had, however, consistently favored
enlargement of the suffrage, removal of restrictione on civil liberties, and
enhancement of the power of parliamentary institutions.

Shortly after its organization, the Shakaits put forward a number of concrete
proposals for basic reform. Among the reforms proposed were: the enactment of a
democratic constitution according to the will of the people; the reduction of the
Emperor's prerogatives; the abolition of the imperial power to issue emergency
ordinances; the amendment of the Imperial House Law; the abolition of the Privy
Council and the office of Lord Privy Seal; abolition of the peerage; the establishment
of cabinet responsibility to the Diet; the elimination of the government's power to.
enforce the budget of the preceding year if the Diet refused to pass the proposed
budget; the retention of a bicameral legislature, with one house to be based on
regional and one on functional representation; the establishment of proportional
representation and of universal suffrage at the age of eighteen; the expansion of
civil liberties; the revision of the constitutional amendment process; and the
1
election of local officials.
In January 1946 the Shakaito put forward 1ts own draft proposals for a
revised constitution, a policy also followed by the Liberal and Progressive
Parties. All of these draft proposals were both brief and vague. of the drafts
of the three major parties, however, that of the Socialists was the most detailed
and represented the greatest departure from tradition. In the Socialist draft
sovereignty was defined as resting in the state, defined as the national community
including the Emperor. The Emperor's powers, moreover, were clearly circumscribed,
the Socialist draft differing from the others in specifying what the Emperor might
do rather than merely enumerating which of his prerogatives were to be abolished.
Thus it was provided that the Prime Minister was to be eppointed by the Emperor,
who was required to abide by the recommendation of the presidents of both houses.
Similarly, the Emperor was to sign treaties and laws approved by the Diet but could

not veto them. The section on the Emperor concluded with the statement that he was
to have no political responsibility and that succession to the throne and establishmont

The Socialist draft provided for a bicameral legislature, with members of the
upper house elected on a functional basie. The Diet was to have the powers of
legislation, of directing and supervising administration, of approving treaties, of
approving state revenue and expenditures, and of introducing amendmente to the
constitution. The lower house was empowered to overrule the veto of the upper on all
legislation, and the Diet as a whole might be dissolved by plebiscite. A standing
committee was to act for the Diet during recesses. The cabinet was to be responsible
to the Diet. Its functions were to include the conduct of foreign relations, internal
administration, law enforcement, and appointment of officials. The Privy Council was
to be abolished.
The Socialist draft's bill of rights provided for inviolable civil liberties.
In addition, the draft contained a number of provisions with regard to the obligations
owed by the state to the people, particularly in the economic field, and subjected
the right of owmership to limitations for the general welfare. No provision was made
for judicial review. Judges were to be independent and appointed by the cabinet

II. THE NIPPON KYÖSANTÖ (COMMUNIST PARTY OF JAPAN)
A.
Orgenization of the Party
1. Leadership. The revival of Communist activities on Japanese soil began
with the SCAP directive of October 1945 ordering the release of politicel
prisoners. The leadership of the revived Kyōsantō, like that of the Shakeitō, has
since rested largely in the hands of veteran members of the party. Even before
their release from prison, TOKUDA Kyuichi and SHIGA Yoshio assumed the leadership
of the party and acted as its spokosmen, but 1t was not until December 1945 that
their position was formalized with the election of the Central Committee at the
Fourth National Congress. At this Congress, attended by 500 party members, Tokuda
was elected General Secretary and chairman of the Political Organization Committee,
while Shiga was elected to the seven-member Central Committee.
It was nevertheless generally believed at this time that the supreme leadership
of the party would ultimately be assumed by the exiled Japanese Commmist leader
NOSAKA Sanzo, who, at the time of the Fourth Congress, had not yet returned from
Yenan. The plausibility of this expectation was reinforced by a statement made
by party headquarters at the time of Nosaka's return in January: "We have noted
Comrade Nosaka's newspaper statement that he will work as one of the party members
from now on...we intend to have him as our supreme leader. This is the opinion and
desire of all."1 On the other hand, the fact that the views he erpressed in Yenan,
particularly on the Emperor question, differed significantly from those that had
been advanced by the Nippon Kyosantō in the months preceding his arrival appeared to
be a factor that might militate against Nosaka's elevation to party leadership.

2. Structure. The regulations governing the organization and procedure of the
Kyosanto are, on the whole, similar to those prevailing in Communist parties elsewhere.
They provide for firm control at the top based on a hierarchy of regional, prefectural
and district organizations resting ultimately on the local unit, the cell. Organized
penetration of non-Commumist groups is the responsibility of the fractions set up
wherever three or more Communists are members of a trade union, cooperative,
cultural group, or similar organization. These fractions, in turn, like the cells,
are responsible to the district, prefectural, regional, and central committees.
Decisions of the higher organizations are binding on the lower, and a party decision,
once made, must be obeyed unconditionally, with criticiam possible only within the
party and then on a very limited basis.
According to the Kyosanto constitution, adopted at the Fifth Congress of the
party in February 1946 and amended at the Sixth Congress in December 1947,3 the
national congress is theoretically the highest organ of the party. Meeting once a

3. Membership. Kyōsanto members are defined by the party constitution as those
who accept the party program, enter a party organization, and pay party dues regularly.
Members are under the obligation to abide by party regulations and policy, participate
in party activities, popularize the party and its views by taking part in mass
organizations, and study the works of Marx and Lenin.
Applicants for party membership must be recommended by two Kyosanto members, who
thenceforth are held responsible for their recommendations. Candidates for membership
are diecussed by the cells and must be approved by the district committee and, in
some cases, by the Central Committee before their admission to the party. As this
process indicates, the Kyōsanto, regarding 1tself as a disciplined vanguard group, is
more selective in its membership policy than is usually the case with political
parties. There is some reason to believe, however, that the party, in the interests
of broadening its memberehip, has recently tended to place emphasis upon indoctrination
after rather than before admission to the party. In a Kyosantō round-table in March

B. Strategy and Tactics
1. Introduction. From the time of its revival to the present, the Nippon
Kyosanto has insisted that it seeks to bring about through peaceful democratic
means first the bourgeois democratic revolution and then the socialist revolution.
The publication of the party program following the Fifth Congress was an attempt
to impress this policy on the public mind and to correct what were regarded as
popular misapprehensions concerning Commmist addiction to extreme and immediate
change and to violent and dictatorial methods.
1
Public adherence by the Kyosanto to a policy of peaceful revolution has, however,
neither dispelled popular misgivings with regard to the real intentions of the
Commnist nor prevented dissension within the party as to strategy and tactice.
Party discussion of such problems has been conducted at great length in Communist
publications and has included in its scope wordy and not particularly searching
analyses of the nature of imperialiem in general, of Japanese imperialism in
particular, end of the applicability of Lenin's analysis of the Seven Years' War to
post-surrender Japan.
That the question has also been discussed privately and
perhaps more pointedly may be aesumed, and the rumors of disagreements and potential
aplits in Commmist ranks that appear so frequently in the Japanese press generally
describe such disagreements as revolving around the strategy of peaceful revolution.
The weakness of Jepanese theoretical arguments, in comparison with those published

significance in the party's program. This fact is in part a reflection of the
emotional aura that surrounds any discussion of the Emperor in Japan and in part a
reflection of the prevalent conviction that the Emperor issue is the hub of whatever
conflict may exist between Tokuda and Nosaka.

In its preemble, the Communist draft ascribed the war and the ills that

the draft provided that the abolition of the republican form of government was never
to be the subject of an amendment to the constitution.
The first chapter of the Communist draft defined sovereignty as resting with
the people and called for the operation of the Japanese economy for the stabilization
and improvement of the people's livelihood; the ebolition of the feudalistic land-
hold ing system; the dissolution of the Zaibatsu; and the establishment of regulations
concernine finance and mejor industries. A provision renouncing aggressive war was
also contained in the first chapter.
Under the draft, legielative power was vested in a unicameral National Assembly,
members of which were to be elected for a four-year term by citizens over eighteen
without discrimination regarding residence, property, creed, sex, race, education, or
sociul conditions. Elections were to be direct and secret and based on proportional
ropresentation. Members of the National Assembly were to be required to report
periodically to their constituencies and were to be subject to recall under provisions
to be estahlished by law. The Assembly might be dissolved by a vote of two-thirds
of itą membersnip.

capitalist and fascist concept that is typically anti-foreign, aggressive, and

III. REVIVAL OF THE TRADE-UNION MOVEMENT1
A.
Introduction
In the period since the surrender, the Japanese trade-union movement has grown
rapidly, far outstripping in membership and importance the pre-l940 movement, which,
Ministry survey, of Japan's approximately 9,000,000 wage earners 6,533,954 workers
were organized in registered trade unions. Somewhat less than half of these
organized workers were members of unions affiliated with one of the three trade-
union federatione.3
As in the prewar period, the trade unions, particularly the federations, have
shown strong interest in political activity. A conspicuous manifestation of this
interest has been the tendency to utilize the strike as a weapon against the
government as well as a technique of labor dispute. More important in the long run,
perhaps, as an expression of labor's political interest are the ties that have been
forged between the unions and the Shakaitō and the Kyōsantō.
Both the Socialists and the Communists have, of course, been active in seeking
trade-union support for their respective parties. In the rivalry between the
Shakaito and the Kyōsantō for influence in the trade-union movement the Shakaitō
gained an initial advantage from the fact that it numbers among its members most
of the experienced trade-union leaders who dominated the important unions of
prewar Japan. The Kyōsantō, on the other hand, benefited by the fact that in
prewar Japan the great mase of labor was unorganized, enabling the Communists to
capitalize upon inexperience in trade-mion procedures as well as upon rank-and-file

PART THREE: MAJOR DEVELOPMENTS IN LEFT-WING POLITICS, 1945-46
I. THE POPULAR FRONT MOVEMENT BEFORE THE ELECTIONS OF APRIL 10, 1946
A.
Commmmist Attempts to Create a Popular Front
1. Introduotion. The Comuniste in Japan have to a considerable extent eseumed
the initiative in the movement for a popular front. Although in the period before
the elections of 1946 their proposals had fairly wide press support as well as the
sympathy of many left-wing Socialiste, the results of their offorts since that time
have been negligible. In these efforts to establish a popular front, the Commmmists
have employed a variety of methods, sometimes singly and at other times in
combination. Among these methods have been: attempts to secure Socialist
agreement to a united front between the two parties as a basis for the subsequent
organization of a popular front including all "democratic" elements;1 attempts to
secure a united front between Commmist-and Socialist-influenced workers' and
peasants' organizations; attempts to secure a popular front for action on such
specifio issues as the food crisis; and attempts to organize individual demonstrations
on a popular front basis. Tactics employed by the Commumists have ranged from
attempts to secure the Socialist leaderahip's official approval of the popular front
principle to offorts to influence the Socialist left wing and the rank and file in
favor of a popular front as a means of putting pressure on the party leadership.
2. The Jimmin Kaiho Remme1 (Peoplo's Emancipation League). In October 1945,
when both parties were still in the organizational state, the Japanese Commmists
approached the Socialiste with a popular front proposal that was rejected by the
latter on the grounds that no such suggestion could be antertained until the two

agreement between proletarian parties on certain basic issues and lines of action
constitutes a united frant; an extension of this agreement to bourgeois parties n
and other non-working-class organizations constitutes a popular front. Seo

II. THE LEFT AND THE FORMATION OF THE YOSHIDA CABINET
A.
The General Eloction of Apr11 10, 1946
1. Introduction. The election of April 10, 1946 offered the newly organized
Japanese political parties their first opportumity to test their popular support.
Moreover, although Japan was still operating under the Meiji Constitution, which
established no formal connection between the composition of the Diet and the
composition of the cabinet, it was evident that occupation policies had changed the
situation in fact if not in form and, therefore, that the results of the election
might have considerable effect upon the nature of the post-election cabinet. For
the proletarian parties the election was particularly significant as their first
opportunity to campaign untrammeled by government prejudice and police interferance.
The Shakaito's postponement of its decision on the popular front made it
inevitable that the two major proletarian parties should run independent campaigns.
It was obvious also that the results of the election would be of considerable
importance in determining the attitude of the Socialists toward cooperation with
the Communists.
2. Socialist Policy. In December, when active campaigning began, the Socialists
were fairly conservative in their nominating policy. At a meeting of the Party
Election Committee on December 14, it was decided that the party would put approximately
200 candidates in the field. Candidates were to be recommended by prefectural
headquarters and approved by the Central Executive Committee; their number was not to
exceed one third of the total seats to be filled in any single constituency except
in such areas as Tokyo, where the party enjoyed unusual strength; and they were to
be assisted by party headquartors, which would provide campaign literature and
By the beginming of January the Socialists had nominated about 165 candidates.
The issuance of the SCAP purge directive on January 4, however, caused the Socialists
to reexamine their nomination policy in the light of the improvement in their
1. Mainichi Shimbun, December 15, 1945; Nippon Times, December 16, 1945.
RESTRICTED

=== Page 468 === (confidence 0.99)
-143-
RESTRICTED
competitive position that resulted from the fact that, as compared with their major
opponents, the Liberals and the Progressives, the Socialists could expect to lose
but little strength in a drastic purge. At this time, therefore, the Central
Executive Committee decided to increase the mmber of party candidates to about
300.1 When the nominations closed, the Shakaito had given its official support to
In the election campaign the Shakaito adopted as its slogan "Rise or Fall;
Socialism or Capitaliam," arguing that only through adoption of the Socialist
program? could Japan survive. The Socialists were careful, however, to emphasize
their allegiance to the principle of gradualiam. Thus KATAYAMA Tetsu declared:
"First of all a representative government is to be established
through which socialization is to be executed to avoid unnecessary
confusion which is inevitably brought about when the process of
socialization is effected by a violent revolution. To achieve this
objective Parliament is to be radically reconstructed to truly
represent the public will Furthermore, special attention is needed
in making a decision on where to begin socialization. Thus, coal,
iron and fertilizer industries, banking, electric generation and
transportation constitute the enterprises which are to be placed
under national management, first of all. This, however, is not to
mean either the free confiscation of private property by the
Government or the despotiem of the proletariat. The procedure of
nationalization is to be deliberately considered by Parliament,
which is the highest inatitution of legislation in a democratic
state."4

B. Major Issues Affecting Lart-Wing Activities in the Cabinet Formation Period
1. Political Background of Left-Wing Activities. The results of the election,
which gave no single party a majority of seats in the Diet, made it apparent that a
coalition would be the essential prerequisite to the formation of a cabinet with
some proapect for stability. The similarity of the background and attitudes of
the Liberals and Progressives may perhaps have mede inevitable their ultimate
cooperation in the formation of a government. Rivalries and ambitions, to some
extent inherited from the prewar period, were sufficiently strong, however, to
lead each of the two conservative parties to look with some interest on the
prospect of joint action with a third party at the erpense of its loading
competitor or even upon the possibility of a three-party coalition. In this
situation, the bargaining power of the Socialist was fairly strong. Their ability
to use it, however, was diminished by the issues of principle upon which the party
was split, issues in which the question of collaboration with bourgeois parties as
against collaboration with the Communists played an important part.
In all, forty days were consumed in the negotiations required to organize a
cabinet. The negotiations went through several stages. The firat began immediately
after the April 10 election with Premier SHIDEHARA Kijuro's attampt to remain in
office and ended on April 22 with Shidehara's resignation partly as a result of the
opposition of the Four-Party Committee organized by the Socialists, Liberals,
Cooperatives, and Communists.
From April 22 until the disqualification of Liberal President HAToYAMA Ichiro
on May 4, the Liberals took the lead in seeking to organize a coalition cabinet.
During vnis period an agreement, fairly limited in natur was reached between the
Liberals and the Socialists, and Shidehara prepared to recommend Hatoyama to the
Eperor.
Following Hatoyama's disqualification on May 4, the initiative passed to the
Socialists and the Progressives, with each party seeking to secure Liberal cooperation
on 1ta own terme. The Socialists made no headway in this endeavor, however, end on

The final stage began on May 16, when YOSHIDA Shigeru received the imperial
mandate. After six additional daye of negotiations, the Yoshida cabinet, roprosenting

2. The Coalition Issue. The coalition issue gave rise to a great deal of
controversy within the Shakaitō Central Executive Committee, which conducted all
Socialist negotiations during this period. Three factions emerged: a left wing opposed
to coalition with either the Liborals or the Progressives and in general sympathy with
Communist popular front proposals; a right wing that favored coalition even with the
Progressives; and a center group opposed to coalition with the Progressives but
somewhat inclined toward cooperation with the Liberals, especially if the latter were
willing to accept Socialist leadership. The coalitionists argued in general that the
1ssue before Japan at the time was not a choice between capitaliam and socialiam and
that the Socialists would be able to bring about the achievement of at least some of
their aims by obtaining representation in the government. To this their opponents
replied that the attainment of a working parliamentary system would be dependent

The first important controversy over the coalition isasue arose with Shidehara's

3. The Popular Front Issue. It is evident from the events that preceded the
Socialist decision of May 9 that the popular front issue, although never decisive,
assumed some importance in this decision and the negotiations that preceded it.
The proponents of the popular front, both Commmists and left-wing Socialists,
employed two tactics to advance their aims: the perpetuation of the Four-Party
Committee and the expansion of its euthority against the opposition of the Liberals
and right-wing Socialists; and the organization of mass meetings and demonstrations
of all kinds to exert pressure on Shidehara to recommend a popular front cabinet and
on the Socialists to seek to form one. Neither of these tactics, of course, was
particularly successful in achieving its ultimate aim. The Four-Party Comittee was
an unlikely source for serious political leadership not only because of the extreme
diversity of ite composition but also because the relative weight of a potential
Liberal-Progressive combination was so great in comparison with that of eny possible
Socialist-centered combination as to make major concessions on the part of the
Liberals unnecessary. Popular pressure in the form in which it was utilized by
the Communists and left-wing Socialists during this period, moreover, was not
particularly effective and ultimately was condemmed by SCAP.
Nevertheless, by the time the Yoshida cabinet was actually installed, proponents
of the popular front could derive comfort from the fact that the Shakaito had
committed itself to an opposition role in the Diet and, more emphatically than in
the past, to the organization of a popular front.

A. The Kyukoku Minshu Sensen Remmei (Democratic Front to Save the Nation)
1. Renewal of Socialist Activities. On January 16, 1946, the Shakaitō Contral
Committee had decided to postpone consideration of the united front issue until
after the elections and on January 29 had reeffirmed this decision. On May 3 the
question was raised once again by KATo Kanju in a meeting of the Shakaitō Central
Executive Committee. At this time, Kato proposed that the Communists, the
Cooperatives, trade unions, farmers' groups, and cultural organizations be invited
to participate in a front that would have as its objectives democratization of
Japan, solution of the food crisis, prevention of inflation, solution of the
A meeting of the Socialist Diet members on May ll marked the beginning of
active Shakaitǒ efforts for the formation of a united front. The desire to take
concrete action was stimulated by dissatisfaction with the policy pursued by the
Central Executive Committee during the coalition negotiations. A resolution
opposing coalition with the conservative parties was passed, and the adoption of
a popular front policy was approved in principle. At the same time the initiative
in presenting concrete plans was taken by MORITo Tatsuo, who proposed the
organization of a front to achieve the social revolution by peaceful and
democratic means. To emphasize its essentially patriotic character, Morito suggested
that the new movement be entitled Kyukoku Minshu Sensen Remmei (Democratic Front to
This proposal was adopted and shortly thereafter a committee on

The Minshu Sensen Sokushinkai operated on two basic premises. The first
was that neither the Shakaito nor the Kyosanto could claim to represent fully the
masses of the people and, therefore, in any united front, mass organizations of an
economic and cultural nature should be accorded a position of equality with the
political parties. The second was that, under existing conditions in Japan,
where political power was exercised by feudalistic and bureaucratic government
officials rather than by the Diet, it would be futile to struggle only for control
of the Diet and, therefore, the struggle for democracy should also be carried on
through the direct participation of non-political organizations.

3. The Shakeitō Plan of May 26. Discussions in the Shakaito united front

on May 26, the committee accepted a compromise proposal drawn up by Morito. The
program of the Socialist-proposed Kyukoku Minshu Sensen Remmei, like Morito's
previous statements, emphasized the achievement of a democratic social movement
by peaceful means. Morito's plan for the structure of the new organization made
concessions to proponents of the inclusion of trade unions, but insured control by
the political parties.
According to Morito's plan, the executive body of the new organization was to
be composed of two sections, the Diet Section and the Popular Movement Section.

IV. THE RENEWAL OF COALITION OVERTURES, DECEMBER 1946 - JANUARY 1947
A.
Introduction
The December-January cabinet crisis in Japan was, in some respects, similar to
the 40-day period that preceded the formetion of the Yoshida cabinet in May 1946.
In both periods the Shakaitō was rent by internal controversy over the issue of
cooperation with the conservative parties; Communists and left-wing Socialists alike
utilized widespread labor discontent to put pressure on right-wing Socialists and
on the government for the formation of a Socialist-centered cabinet; the similarities
between the Liberals and Progressives were sufficiently strong to outweigh their
differences and to leed them to ultimate cooperation; and the formation of a Socialist
or Socialist-centered cabinet was widely demanded by the press.
The differences between the two periods, although less striking, were of some
importance. In the first place, the issue of a united front between the Socialists
and Commmists, which played so important a role in the earlier crisis, did not arise
in the latter period, when the Communists were politically isolated, exerting their
influence through the trade unions rather than through the party and its Diet
representatives. Secondly, internal divisions within the two conservative parties
had become considerably stronger, and the Progressives, particularly the group led
by INukAI Ken, had in their program moved somewhat closer to the Socialists.
B.
The Movement for the Dissolution of the Diet
1.
The Pressure for a New Election. Before the promulgation of the new
Japanese Constitution on November 3, l946, sentiment in favor of calling a now
general eloction before May 3, l947 (when the constitution was to go into effect)
was exhibited principally by the Socialists and Communists, but was shared to some
extent by groups in the government parties. By early November, however, the
Yoshida cabinet had made clear 1ts disinclination to call a new election and its
desire to remain in office until the signing of the peace treaty. On November 4,
the cabinet announced a six-point program that left no doubt regarding its hope for
a long-torm tonure.

free to make coalition offers to the opposition parties.

C. Coalition Negotiations, January 4 - January 17, 1947
1.
Conservative Party Attitudes toward a Coalition Government. With the defeat
of the dissolution motion, the initiative passed to the conservative parties. Despite
the fact that the Liberals and Progressives controlled the Diet and, therefore, on
the surface had no real need to seek the support of the Socialists, a number of
factors led many within the ranks of both parties, but especially among the
Progressives, to look with favor upon the idea of a three-party coalition. Labor
unrest, which had been inteneified by a steadily deteriorating economic situation,
might be mitigated by the inclusion of Socialists in the cabinet; cleavages within
the two conservative parties and friction between them had contributed to the
development of a stalemate within the cabinet on economic policy; and the younger
Progressives, under the leadership of INUKAI Ken, had come increasingly to desire
the adoption of an economic policy that, although not calling for outright
socialization, supported the principles of a planmod and controlled economy.
Several weeks of controverey ensued, with the Liberals in general opposing
proposala for e three-party coalition. At a cabinet meeting on January 4, however,
Premier Yoshida stated that it was his conviction that the economic crisis could not
be alleviated by the simple expedient of reorganizing the two-party cabinet, as had
been proposed by the Liberals, and that the cabinet must alter its economic policies
2
and seek coalition with the Socialists.

3. The Second Rupture. On the morning of January 29 the heads of the three
parties met. It was soon obvious that Yoshida, like the Socialists, had not
retreated significantly from his original terms. Yoshida's offer provided for the
immediate resignation of the cabinet and the organization of a new government based
on a three-party coalition. Ishibashi, Yoshida declared, would remain in the
cabinet; Katayama would become Minister without Portfolio; Hirano, Minister of
Reconstruction; Matsuoka, Minister of Labor; Yonekubo or Morito, Minister of
Commerce and Industry.3 That afternoon the Shakaito Central Executive Committee
reorganization of his cabinet on the existing Liberal-Progressive basis.
4. The Prohibition of the February 1 General Strike. Although Yoshida had
succeeded in reorganizing his cabinet by January 3l, only the presence of SĆAP
averted acute crisis in the relations between the government and its dissatisfied
employees. In part motivated by the belief that no satisfactory setilement could
be reacted with a government regarded as reactionary even by moderate unions, the
disputing workors, increasingly under the influence of Communists and Communist
sympathizers, became ever more uncompromising in their response to the mediation
proposals of the Central Labor Relations Committee. SCAP pressure succeeded in
bringing the government to a more conciliatory position late in January, but
failed to have a corresponding effect on the government workors' unions. On

E. The Aftermath
1. Introduction. With the immediate pressure for overthrow of the Yoshida
cabinet diminiehed by the imminence of a general election, the Sanbetsu turned its
attention to perpetuating and expanding the degree of trade-union unity that had
been achieved in the anti-cabinet and joint struggle committees. At the same
time that greater unity was being sought -- and superficially achieved -- among
the trade-unions, the farmers' union was undergoing ite firat serious split,
precipitated in part by opposition to Hirano's activities during the coalition
negotiations and in part by the issue of Communist influence.
2. Organization of the Zenroren (Zenkoku Rōdokumia1 Renraku Kyōgikai --
